Strong cosmic censorship for the spherically symmetric Einstein-Maxwell-charged-Klein-Gordon system with positive Λ\Lambda: stability of the Cauchy horizon and H1H^{1} extensions

Flavio Rossetti ††thanks: E-mail address: flavio.rossetti@tecnico.ulisboa.pt Affiliation: CAMGSD, Departamento de Matemática, Instituto Superior Técnico IST, Universidade de Lisboa UL, Avenida Rovisco Pais 1, 1049-001 Lisboa, Portugal
Abstract

We investigate the interior of a dynamical black hole as described by the Einstein-Maxwell-charged-Klein-Gordon system of equations with a cosmological constant, under spherical symmetry. In particular, we consider a characteristic initial value problem where, on the outgoing initial hypersurface, interpreted as the event horizon ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+} of a dynamical black hole, we prescribe: a) initial data asymptotically approaching a fixed sub-extremal Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter solution; b) an exponential Price law upper bound for the charged scalar field.

After showing local well-posedness for the corresponding first-order system of partial differential equations, we establish the existence of a Cauchy horizon 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+} for the evolved spacetime, extending the bootstrap methods used in the case Λ=0\Lambda=0 by Van de Moortel [Moo18]. In this context, we show the existence of C0C^{0} spacetime extensions beyond 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+}. Moreover, if the scalar field decays at a sufficiently fast rate along ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+}, we show that the renormalized Hawking mass remains bounded for a large set of initial data. With respect to the analogous model concerning an uncharged and massless scalar field, we are able to extend the range of parameters for which mass inflation is prevented, up to the optimal threshold suggested by the linear analyses by Costa-Franzen [CF17] and Hintz-Vasy [HV17].

In this no-mass-inflation scenario, which includes near-extremal solutions, we further prove that the spacetime can be extended across the Cauchy horizon with continuous metric, Christoffel symbols in Lloc2L^{2}_{\text{loc}} and scalar field in Hloc1H^{1}_{\text{loc}}.

By generalizing the work by Costa-Girão-Natário-Silva [CGNS18] to the case of a charged and massive scalar field, our results reveal a potential failure of the Christodoulou-Chruściel version of the strong cosmic censorship under spherical symmetry.

1 Introduction

1.1 An overview of the model

The present work concerns the system of equations describing a spherically symmetric Einstein-Maxwell-charged-Klein-Gordon model with positive cosmological constant Λ\Lambda, namely:

{Ric​(g)−12​R​(g)​g+Λ​g=2​(TEM+Tϕ),(Einstein’s equations)dF=0,d⋆F=⋆J,(Maxwell’s equations)(Dμ​Dμ−m2)​ϕ=0,(Klein-Gordon equation)\begin{cases}\text{Ric}(g)-\frac{1}{2}\text{R}(g)\,g+\Lambda g=2\left(T^{\text{EM}}+T^{\phi}\right),&\textit{(Einstein's equations)}\\[3.00003pt] dF=0,\quad d\star F=\star J,&\textit{(Maxwell's equations)}\\[3.00003pt] \left(D_{\mu}D^{\mu}-m^{2}\right)\phi=0,&\textit{(Klein-Gordon equation)}\end{cases} (1.1)

where

Tμ​νEM=gα​β​Fα​μ​Fβ​ν−14​gμ​ν​Fα​β​Fα​βT^{\text{EM}}_{\mu\nu}=g^{\alpha\beta}F_{\alpha\mu}F_{\beta\nu}-\frac{1}{4}g_{\mu\nu}F^{\alpha\beta}F_{\alpha\beta}

is the energy-momentum tensor of the electromagnetic field,

Tμ​νϕ=Re⁡(Dμ​ϕ​Dν​ϕ¯)−12​gμ​ν​(Dα​ϕ​Dα​ϕ¯+m2​|ϕ|2)T^{\phi}_{\mu\nu}=\operatorname{Re}\left(D_{\mu}\phi\overline{D_{\nu}\phi}\right)-\frac{1}{2}g_{\mu\nu}\left(D_{\alpha}\phi\overline{D^{\alpha}\phi}+m^{2}|\phi|^{2}\right)

is the energy-momentum tensor of the charged scalar field and

Jμ=−i​q2​(ϕ​Dμ​ϕ¯−ϕ¯​Dμ​ϕ)J_{\mu}=-\frac{iq}{2}\left(\phi\overline{D_{\mu}\phi}-\overline{\phi}D_{\mu}\phi\right)

is the current appearing in Maxwell’s equations. The above system will be presented in full detail in section 2.

The main objective of our work is to study the evolution problem associated to the partial differential equations (PDEs) (1.1), with respect to initial data prescribed on two transversal characteristic hypersurfaces. Along one of these hypersurfaces, the initial data are specified to mimic the expected behaviour of a charged, spherically symmetric black hole, approaching11 1 In an appropriate sense, which will be specified rigorously during our study. a sub-extremal Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter solution and interacting with a charged and (possibly) massive scalar field. This scenario is essentially encoded in the requirement of an exponential decay for such a scalar field along the event horizon in terms of an Eddington-Finkelstein type of coordinate, i.e. an exponential Price law upper bound. The evolved data then describe the interior of a dynamical black hole. A key point of our study regards the existence of a Cauchy horizon and of metric extensions beyond it, in different classes of regularity and most notably in Hloc1H^{1}_{\text{loc}}. An overview of our results is given in section 1.2.

This problem arises naturally as a consequence of a decades-long debate on the mathematical treatment of black hole spacetimes. Already in the case Λ=0\Lambda=0, it was observed that the celebrated Kerr and Reissner-Nordström solutions to the Einstein equations share a daunting property: the future domain of dependence22 2 We define the future domain of dependence of a spacelike hypersurface SS as the set of points pp such that every past-directed, past-inextendible causal curve starting at pp intersects SS [Nat21]. of complete, regular, asymptotically flat, spacelike hypersurfaces is future-extendible in a smooth way. This translates into a failure of classical determinism33 3 The lack of global uniqueness can occur without any loss of regularity of the solution metric, even though the Einstein equations are hyperbolic, up to their diffeomorphism invariance. See [Daf03] for a discussion of this phenomenon. which is in sharp contrast with the Schwarzschild case, where analogous extensions are forbidden even in the continuous class [DS18, Sbi18]. On the other hand, observers crossing a Cauchy horizon44 4 That is the boundary of the future domain of dependence of a complete Cauchy hypersurface in the extended spacetime manifold. We refer the reader to the introduction of [CGNS18] for a discussion on the topic and to [CI93] for constructions of specific non-isometric extensions. are generally expected to experience a blueshift instability [Pen68, SP73], leading to the blow-up of dynamical quantities and thus rescuing the deterministic principle.55 5 In this context, reserving a guaranteed, ominous future for an observer in the black hole interior is preferable to a lack of predictability! The instability is related to the possibility of having an unbounded amount of energy associated to test waves propagating in such a universe, as measured along the Cauchy horizon.66 6 At the level of geometric optics, [Pen68] asserts: “As [an observer crossing the Cauchy horizon 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+}] looks out at the universe that he is ‘leaving behind’, he sees, in one final flash, as he crosses 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+}, the entire later history of the rest of his ‘old universe’ ”. See also Fig. 1.

The subsequent heuristics paved the way to the first formulation of the strong cosmic censorship conjecture (SCCC), which, roughly speaking, asserted that all solutions to the Einstein equations that violate classical determinism are unstable under suitable perturbations.

An outstanding amount of work has been done in the last 50 years to study the blueshift instability and the validity of the SCCC, revealing the subtleties of the topic. On the one hand, it has been studied to which extent the blueshift instability, firstly described as a heuristic linear phenomenon, can affect the picture of gravitational collapse in the full non-linear regime. At the same time, substantial progress has been made to render the SCCC into a precise mathematical statement.

Numerical and analytical studies indeed showed that the original description of the blueshift instability had to be reconciled with the dispersive effects that influence linear waves. A series of works on this problem showed that scalar perturbations are expected to decay along the event horizon of black holes, at a rate which, essentially, is exponential in the case Λ>0\Lambda>0 [Dya15, DR07, Mav23], inverse polynomial in the case Λ=0\Lambda=0 [Pri72, GPP94, DR05, AAG18, Hin22] and logarithmic for Λ<0\Lambda<0 [HS13]. This behaviour is known as Price’s law.

Applying this insight to the full non-linear problem, however, is technically challenging. A turning point was the adoption of the Einstein-Maxwell-(real) scalar field model to study black hole interiors [Daf03], following previous work by Israel and Poisson [PI90]. Indeed, such a spherically symmetric (non-linear) toy model is able to efficiently describe the effects of Price’s law and of back-reaction, while at the same time capturing essential traits of the general setting. The addition of a scalar field, in particular, is motivated by the hyperbolic properties expected from the Einstein equations, and removes the constraints imposed by Birkhoff’s theorem. Inspired by this setting, the analysis of the non-linear problem in the absence of spherical symmetry was initiated only in the past few years [DL17]. We will review relevant past work in section 1.4.

Subsequently, several formulations of the SCCC have been advanced, depending on the required regularity of the extended metric as a solution to the Einstein equations. All these versions of the SCCC concern generic77 7 The notion of genericity itself presents additional subtleties. In Christodoulou [Chr99]: one could define an initial data set to be non-generic if it has measure zero, provided that a suitable probability measure is defined on the infinite-dimensional set of initial data. However, even when such a framework is available, computing the measure of a specific set might be arduous: in the same work, the author noticed that already in non-relativistic mechanics there exist sets of initial data for the NN–body problem, N≥3N\geq 3, leading to collision singularities in finite time and whose probability measure is still unknown. initial data.

While the existence of generic C2C^{2} extensions represents a failure of determinism in the strongest sense, their absence does not prevent the occurrence of less regular extensions. Moreover, the C2C^{2} level of regularity is seldom the most natural requirement. A discontinuous energy-momentum tensor in the Einstein equations typically appears for many physically relevant matched spacetimes, and can be related to solutions endowed with a C1C^{1} metric.

On the other hand, the lack of continuous extensions entails unbounded geodesic deviation when reaching the boundary of the future domain of dependence (this is what occurs at the r=0r=0 singularity in the Schwarzschild spacetime [Sbi18]). A further case is the Hloc1H^{1}_{\text{loc}} (Christodoulou-Chruściel) regularity, which is the minimal requirement to make sense of extensions as weak solutions to the Einstein equations (see also [CGNS18, DS18, Chr09, Chr91]), even though local well–posedness is not known to hold in this case [KRS15]. Weaker formulations can also be considered [Rei23]. We stress that showing the existence of an extension beyond the Cauchy horizon does not suffice to verify that such an extension satisfies the Einstein equations, but it is however a prerequisite for such a task.88 8 See also [GL19] for an approach to this problem in the extremal case. Moreover, proving that a particular, e.g. C0C^{0}, extension is not C1C^{1} does not forbid the existence of other distinct C1C^{1} extensions. An efficient way to rule out the latter might be to show the blow-up of a geometric C1C^{1} quantity. This is the case of the Hawking mass in the works [PI90, Daf05a, CGNS18], for instance.

We stress that each formulation of the SCCC has to take into account the symmetries of the system and the nature of the adopted initial value problem, see also section 1.3 for a related discussion. Although we do not show that the initial conditions of our system arise from the evolution of initial data from an appropriate spacelike Cauchy hypersurface, our work provides strong evidence against general formulations of the SCCC. In particular, the content of this article is strictly related to the following conjectures.

Conjecture 1.1 (C0C^{0} formulation of the SCCC for the Einstein-Maxwell-charged-Klein-Gordon system with Λ>0\Lambda>0, under spherical symmetry)

Let Σ\Sigma be a regular, compact (without boundary),99 9 The case of S3S^{3} is often considered in the literature. Non-compact, “asymptotically de Sitter” hypersurfaces can also be examined. See also Fig. 3 for an overview on potential global structures. spacelike hypersurface. Let us prescribe generic (in the spherically symmetric class) initial data on Σ\Sigma, for the Einstein-Maxwell-charged-Klein-Gordon system with Λ>0\Lambda>0. Then, the future maximal globally hyperbolic development1010 10 Which is, roughly speaking, the largest Lorentzian manifold determined by the evolution of Cauchy data via the Einstein equations. See [Rin09] for a precise definition. of such initial data cannot be locally extended as a Lorentzian manifold endowed with a continuous metric.

Conjecture 1.2 (Hloc1H^{1}_{\text{loc}} formulation of the SCCC for the Einstein-Maxwell-charged-Klein-Gordon system with Λ>0\Lambda>0, under spherical symmetry)

Let Σ\Sigma be a regular, compact (without boundary), spacelike hypersurface. Let us prescribe generic (in the spherically symmetric class) initial data on Σ\Sigma, for the Einstein-Maxwell-charged-Klein-Gordon system with Λ>0\Lambda>0. Then, the future maximal globally hyperbolic development of such initial data cannot be locally extended as a Lorentzian manifold endowed with a continuous metric and Christoffel symbols in Hloc1H^{1}_{\text{loc}}.

In particular, this work contributes to fill a gap in the literature by suggesting a negative resolution to conjecture 1.1 and, more significantly, a negative resolution, for a large subset of the parameter space, to conjecture 1.2. Being a natural generalization of [CGNS18] (but notice that the coupled scalar field is now charged and possibly massive) and [Moo18] (in our case, however, Λ>0\Lambda>0, thus the Price law is exponential rather than inverse polynomial), we take these works as starting points for our analysis. In section 1.4 we review previous relevant work and compare the techniques we employed with those of [CGNS18] and [Moo18].

1.2 Summary of the main results

The main conclusions of our work can be outlined as follows. We first study the characteristic initial value problem (IVP) for the first-order system related to (1.1) (this corresponds to equations (2.20)–(2.33)) and establish its local well-posedness, modulo diffeomorphism invariance (see theorem 3.2 and proposition 3.4). We then provide a novel proof of the extension criterion for the first-order system (theorem 4.1), demanding less regularity on the initial data as compared to the analogous result in [Kom13, theorem 1.8] for the second-order system.

Subsequently, we show the equivalence between the first-order and the second-order Einstein-Maxwell-charged-Klein-Gordon systems (see remark 3.5) under additional regularity of the initial data, which we assume for the remaining part of our work. Finally, we assess the global uniqueness of the dynamical black hole under investigation, and its consequences for SCCC, in the following classes of regularity.

We stress that the range of parameters allowing for H1H^{1} extensions is not expected to depend on the charge of the scalar field. In particular, our methods can be applied to the uncharged case as well.

1.3 Strong cosmic censorship in full generality

The results of our analysis show that the main conclusion of [CGNS18] is still valid when we add a charge (and possibly mass) to the coupled scalar field: according to the state of the art of SCCC, the potential scenarios that lead to a violation of determinism in the case 𝚲>𝟎\bm{\Lambda>0} cannot be ruled out.

To explain how to reach this conclusion, we first illustrate the connection between our results and conjecture 1.2, and then the relation between the latter and other formulations of SCCC.

The results presented in section 1.2 stem from the evolution of initial data from two transversal null hypersurfaces, one of which modelling the event horizon of a dynamical black hole. This suggests that the black hole we take under consideration has already formed at the beginning of the evolution.1414 14 Notice that the interior and exterior problems can be treated separately, due to domain of dependence arguments, and the exterior region in this context was proved to be stable in [Hin18], with respect to gravitational and electromagnetic perturbations.

Strictly speaking, however, SCCC constrains the admissible future developments of spacelike hypersurfaces, on which generic initial data are specified. Although we are not committed to any specific global structure, it is useful to think of the characteristic IVP of section 2.1 as arising from suitable (compact or non-compact) initial data prescribed in the black hole exterior (see also Fig. 3). The reason why we believe that our results are relevant to SCCC is that the initial data we prescribe for our characteristic IVP are compatible with numerical solutions obtained in the exterior of Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter black holes. Such results are also expected to hold for perturbations of such black holes, due to the non-linear stability result [Hin18].

In particular, our vv coordinate can be compared to half of the outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein coordinate of [CCDHJ18a] (see appendix B). This can be used to see that, according to the same article, condition (1.4) can be (numerically) attained at the linear level: s>K−s>K_{-} (i.e. β=s2​K−>12\beta=\frac{s}{2K_{-}}>\frac{1}{2}, in the language of [CCDHJ18a]) for linear waves propagating in the exterior of near-extremal (i.e. ρ\rho close to 1) Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter black holes. This result is also expected to hold on dynamical black holes sufficiently close to Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter, as the one we analyse. Indeed, notice that on a fixed background ss is equal, up to a multiplying factor, to the spectral gap of the Laplace-Beltrami operator □g\square_{g}. If we denote by QNM the set of the quasinormal modes of the reference black hole, the spectral gap can also be expressed by

infω∈QNMIm⁡(ω)<0(−Im⁡(ω)).\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}\omega\in\text{QNM}\\ \operatorname{Im}(\omega)<0\end{subarray}}\left(-\operatorname{Im}(\omega)\right).

In particular, ss depends on the black hole parameters. At the same time, [Hin18] shows that, under small perturbations, the parameters of the perturbed solution are sufficiently close to the initial ones.

Therefore, once the numerical results of [CCDHJ18a] are verified rigorously and extended to the non-linear case, a mathematical proof for the validity of (1.4) would in principle be possible, leading to a negative resolution of conjecture 1.2.

On the other hand, conjectures 1.1 and 1.2 regard initial data which are generic in the spherically symmetric class, but non-generic in the much larger moduli space of all possible initial configurations. In particular, when we talk about SCCC under spherical symmetry, the validity or failure of such a conjecture does not automatically settle the non-spherically symmetric problem. Nonetheless, due to analogies with the conformal structure of a Kerr-Newman spacetime, it is widely believed [Daf03, Daf05a, CGNS18, DL17] that results obtained in the charged spherically symmetric context can provide vital evidence to either uphold or refute formulations of SCCC in absence of spherical symmetry.1515 15 The case of uncharged black holes, however, needs to be inspected separately. See the numerical study [DERS18] for Kerr-de Sitter.

A larger moduli space can also be achieved by working in a rougher class of initial data. In [DS18], where global uniqueness is investigated at the linear level, the following is proved: given initial data (ψ0,ψ0′)∈Hloc1×Lloc2(\psi_{0},\psi_{0}^{\prime})\in H^{1}_{\text{loc}}\times L^{2}_{\text{loc}} to the linear wave equation □g​ψ=0\square_{g}\psi=0 on a sub-extremal Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter black hole, with data prescribed on a complete spacelike hypersurface, ψ\psi cannot be extended across the Cauchy horizon in Hloc1H^{1}_{\text{loc}}. This means that, if the numerical results [CCDHJ18] obtained in the exterior of Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter black holes were to be proved rigorously, the initial data leading to a potential failure of SCCC could be ignored, because they are non-generic in this larger set of rough initial configurations. Whether this Sobolev level of regularity for the initial data is “suitable” may well depend on the problem to be studied and is still a topic of discussion in the literature.

1.4 Previous works and outline of the bootstrap method

The case 𝚲=𝟎\bm{\Lambda=0}: after foundational work by Christodoulou [Chr99], Dafermos [Daf03] first laid the framework for the analysis of the SCCC in spherical symmetry via modern PDE methods. With the long-term motivation of probing the stability of the Cauchy horizon for a Kerr black hole,1616 16 We can hardly overestimate the crucial role of the Kerr spacetime in any modern theory of gravity. We refer the reader to [MTW73, part V, part VII] and [KS22] for discussions about the final state conjecture, the stability problem and the astrophysical relevance of this solution. he studied the Einstein-Maxwell-(real) scalar field system as a proxy to the full non-linear problem. This first pioneering work concerned a characteristic initial value problem where Reissner-Nordström initial data (and a zero scalar field) were assumed on the initial outgoing characteristic hypersurface. The direct analogy between the conformal structure of the interior of Kerr and that of the Reissner-Nordström solution indeed supports the choice of the latter model as a representative of the behaviour of the rotating black hole.

Apart from spherical symmetry, two artificial elements are included in this framework: the scalar field is taken real-valued, thus restricting the analysis to solutions expected to arise from two-ended, asymptotically flat, initial data [Kom13]. On the other hand, the scalar field is assumed to vanish identically along the initial outgoing hypersurface, so that Reissner-Nordström initial data are prescribed there.

The latter assumption was replaced in [Daf05a], where the C0C^{0} version of SCCC was proved to be false, conditionally on the validity of a Price law upper bound, which was later seen to hold in [DR05]. In [Daf05a], the C1C^{1} formulation of SCCC was seen to hinge on the validity of a lower bound on the scalar field along the event horizon. The work [LO19], again on the Einstein-Maxwell-(real) scalar field system under spherical symmetry, ascertained the validity of the C2C^{2} formulation of SCCC. This was achieved by proving that an integrated lower bound holds generically for the scalar field and that this leads to a curvature blow-up, identically along the Cauchy horizon.

The first steps towards the analysis of a complex-valued (i.e. charged) and possibly massive scalar field were taken in [Kom13]: this is the model that we denoted as the Einstein-Maxwell-charged-Klein-Gordon system. The work [Kom13], in particular, presented a soft analysis of the future boundary of spacetimes undergoing spherical collapse. More recent work on the SCCC for the same system can be found in [Moo18, Moo22, Moo21, KM22], where continuous spacetime extensions were constructed and several instability results obtained.

The analysis of the full non-linear problem, namely the validity of the SCCC for a Kerr spacetime, was initiated in the seminal work [DL17]. Here, the C0C^{0} formulation of the SCCC was shown to be false, under the assumption of the quantitative stability of the Kerr exterior. The problem is indeed intertwined with stability results of black hole exteriors, object of an intense activity that built on a sequence of remarkable results and notably led, in recent times, to [GKS22, KS21, KS22] for slowly rotating Kerr solutions. Further celebrated results are the non-linear stability of the Schwarzschild family [DHRT21] and, in the case Λ>0\Lambda>0, the non-linear stability of slowly rotating Kerr-Newman-de Sitter black holes [Hin18]. For an overview on the problem and recent contributions both in the linear and non-linear realm, we refer the reader to [AB15, HHV21, Mos20, Gio20, Ben22, Tei20] and references therein.

The case 𝚲>𝟎\bm{\Lambda>0}: Compared to the asymptotically flat scenario, the presence of a positive cosmological constant leads to substantial changes in the causal structure of black hole solutions. A Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter black hole, for instance, presents a spacelike future null infinity and an additional Killing horizon 𝒞+\mathcal{C}^{+} (the cosmological horizon). As a result, scalar perturbations of such a black hole decay exponentially fast along ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+} [Dya15]. This behaviour competes with the blueshift effect expected near the Cauchy horizon and determining a growth, also exponential, of the main perturbed quantities. While SCCC is expected to prevail in the asymptotically flat case (the exponential contribution from blueshift wins over the inverse polynomial tails propagating from the event horizon), the situation drastically changes when Λ>0\Lambda>0. In the latter case, indeed, knowing the exact asymptotic rates of scalar perturbations along the event horizon, and thus determining which of the two exponential contributions is the leading one, is of vital importance to determine the admissibility of spacetime extensions. For instance, a sufficiently rapid decay given by the Price law is expected to overcome the blueshift effect and allow observers to cross the Cauchy horizon without significant obstructions. So far, a quantitative description of the exponents for such a decay is available at the linear level via numerical methods [CCDHJ18, CCDHJ18a, CM22, MTWZZ18], whereas rigorous results are mostly lacking (see however [Hin21] and [HX22] where Kerr and Schwarzschild solutions with positive Λ\Lambda have been studied in the case of small black hole mass or small cosmological constant). In this work, all possible exponential rates along the event horizon are taken into consideration.

Similarly to the case of a zero cosmological constant, the SCCC with Λ>0\Lambda>0 has also been studied via the Einstein-Maxwell-(real) scalar field model. The works [CGNS15, CGNS15a, CGNS17] can be compared to [Daf03]: a characteristic initial value problem was studied, with data on the initial outgoing hypersurface given by the event horizon of a Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter black hole. One of the main novelties of this series of papers is a partition of the black hole interior in terms of level sets of the radius function, rather than curves of constant shifts as in [Daf03, Daf05a] (the latter curves fail to be spacelike when Λ≠0\Lambda\neq 0). These three works deal with a real scalar field, taken identically zero along the event horizon. Conversely, an exponential Price law (both a lower bound and an upper bound) was prescribed in [CGNS18] along the event horizon (compare with [Daf05a]), and generic initial data leading to C0C^{0} extensions were constructed. Conditions to have either Hloc1H^{1}_{\text{loc}} extensions or mass inflation where given in terms of the decay of the scalar field along the event horizon.

The work that we present in the next sections is a natural prosecution of [CGNS18] as it replaces the neutral scalar field with a charged one, whose behaviour along the event horizon is dictated by an exponential Price law upper bound. Differently from [CGNS18], however, we are able to prove stability results in the charged case without requiring a Price law lower bound, and we extend, in a way which is expected to be optimal, the set of parameters ss and ρ\rho that allow for Hloc1H^{1}_{\text{loc}} extensions.

On a more technical level, we stress that the exponential Price law is prescribed as a consequence of the positivity of the cosmological constant. On the other hand, our computations show that the sign of Λ\Lambda does not affect the conclusions of this work.1717 17 One could think of prescribing the exponential Price law upper bound (2.49), while considering Λ≤0\Lambda\leq 0. The results of this paper still hold under this assumptions.

We also mention the numerical works [CCDHJ18, CCDHJ18a], which inspected the effects of linear scalar perturbations on sub-extremal Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter black holes. For a charged scalar field, numerical evolutions suggest that there exist values for the scalar field charge and the final black hole charge for which the (Christodoulou-Chruściel) SCCC is violated at the linear level. A different outcome was found in the Kerr-de Sitter case [DERS18], where numerical results showed that Hloc1H^{1}_{\text{loc}} SCCC is respected in the linear setting. An extension of these results to regions of the Kerr-Newman family was presented in [CM22].

The case 𝚲<𝟎\bm{\Lambda<0} and extremal black holes: recent progress with the investigation of SCCC both for the case Λ<0\Lambda<0 and for extremal black holes can be found, for instance, in [HS13, Keh22, Mos20] and [Are11, AAG23].

Comparison with [Moo18] and [CGNS18]: the present work generalizes the results of [CGNS18] to the case of a charged and (possibly) massive scalar field, without requiring any lower bound1818 18 An (integrated or pointwise) lower bound for the scalar field is generally expected in order to prove instability estimates, such as mass inflation. We will not pursue this direction in our study, even though the estimates we obtain in the black hole interior pave the way to a future analysis of instability results. for it along the initial outgoing characteristic hypersurface. Differently from the neutral case, a charged scalar field is compatible with a more realistic description of gravitational collapse (see Fig. 3 for potential global structures). At the same time, the charged setting requires gauge covariant derivatives, brings additional terms in the equations and generally undermines monotonicity properties due to the fact that the scalar field is now complex-valued. With respect to the real case, additional dynamical quantities, such as the electromagnetic potential AuA_{u} and the charge function QQ, need to be controlled during the evolution. Moreover, the scalar field is expected to oscillate along the event horizon of the dynamical black hole: the pointwise Price law lower bound used in [CGNS18] to prove instability results is too restrictive to be replicated in the current case. The presence of a mass term for the scalar field, on the other hand, allows to describe compact objects formed by massive spin-0 bosons.

In particular, we replace many monotonicity arguments exploited in [CGNS18] with bootstrap methods. In this sense, our work follows the spirit of [Moo18], where the stability of the Cauchy horizon was proved by bootstrapping the main estimates from the event horizon. However, as we will see, the techniques we use to close the bootstrap arguments differ more and more from the ones of [Moo18] as we approach the Cauchy horizon. More specifically, we subdivide the black hole interior into five regions:1919 19 Rather than the six of [CGNS18]. In particular, we do not need to distinguish between the future and the past of the apparent horizon, which is localized in what we now call the redshift region. these are the event horizon, the redshift region, the no-shift region, the early blueshift region and the late blueshift region. The subdivision is given in terms of curves of constant area-radius, as in [CGNS15a, CGNS17, CGNS18]. This partition is loosely analogous to the one performed in [Moo18], which is the source for this nomenclature, in the sense that both constructions measure the redshift and blueshift effects in a similar fashion. This analogy, however, is only meaningful if the different values of the cosmological constant are taken into account (inverse polynomial decay rates need to be replaced by exponential ones and vice versa). Indeed, differently from [Moo18], the exponential Price law in our work gives exponential terms in the main estimates, that compete against the decay rate given by the redshift effect and the exponential growth near the Cauchy horizon, due to blueshift. This is exemplarily represented by the loss of decay in the redshift region, compared to the event horizon, for solutions to the IVP.2020 20 This phenomenon manifests itself in the bounded term c⁡(s)c(s), instead of s∈(0,+∞)s\in(0,+\infty), appearing in the main estimates.

We expand the results of [CGNS18] to the case of a charged and possibly massive scalar field. In particular being able to prove the existence of Hloc1H^{1}_{\text{loc}} extensions beyond the Cauchy horizon in a larger set of black hole parameters, in a way which is expected to be sharp according to the linear theory [CF17, HV17]. We stress that the only restrictions on the scalar field charge qq and mass mm are given by q≠0q\neq 0 and m≥0m\geq 0.

We now summarize the main technical strategies that we adopt in each region of the black hole interior (see also Fig. 4). Here, the quantities r−r_{-} and r+r_{+} represent the radii of the Cauchy horizon and of the event horizon, respectively, of the fixed sub-extremal Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter black hole. We recall that in section 1.2 we presented the coordinates uu and vv and the function Ω2\Omega^{2} (see (1.2)). The function μ\mu is defined in (2.16).

We then obtain an exponentially fast convergence of the main dynamical quantities to those of the reference Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter black hole. We mainly follow [Moo18] for this result (there, the convergence is inverse polynomial since Λ\Lambda is zero).

This is not possible in our case, since such a value is a constant and is equal to R−YR-Y, again due to our construction in terms of constant-radius curves. The soft arguments used in [CGNS18] to propagate the known estimates do not apply here, due to the presence of a non-constant charge function QQ. Therefore, we propagate the main estimates by bootstrap again. The bootstrap technique is different from the one of the previous regions, since we have less control on the quantities ϕ\phi and Du​ϕD_{u}\phi. A key role in the bootstrap argument is played by an estimate on ∂vlog⁡Ω2\partial_{v}\log\Omega^{2}, which we propagate from the event horizon and is used essentially only in this region. This quantity measures, in some sense, the redshift and blueshift effects. It was used repeatedly in [Moo18] to show the existence of C0C^{0} extensions. Furthermore, in contrast with [CGNS18], we are able to obtain a finer control on the H1H^{1} norm of the scalar field. This allows us to provide a larger generic set of initial data, with respect to [CGNS18], for which mass inflation can be prevented and Hloc1H^{1}_{\text{loc}} extensions can be obtained.

The outline of the paper is the following: in section 2 we delve into the main aspects of the characteristic IVP for the Einstein-Maxwell-charged-Klein-Gordon system under spherical symmetry. Well-posedness of the characteristic IVP is investigated in section 3. An extension criterion is given in section 4.

In section 5 we establish quantitative bounds along ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+} for the main PDE variables of the characteristic IVP, and propagate these bounds to the black hole interior by bootstrap. This allows us to prove the stability of 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+} and to construct a continuous spacetime extension at the end of the same section.

In section 6 we provide a sharp condition on the reference sub-extremal black hole to generically prevent the occurrence of mass inflation. Under such an assumption, we also construct an Hloc1H^{1}_{\text{loc}} spacetime extension up to and including the Cauchy horizon.

2 The Einstein-Maxwell-charged-Klein-Gordon system under spherical symmetry

The present work revolves around the system of equations describing a spherically symmetric Einstein-Maxwell-charged-Klein-Gordon model with positive cosmological constant Λ\Lambda:

{Ricμ​ν​(g)−12​R​(g)​gμ​ν+Λ​gμ​ν=2​(Tμ​νEM+Tμ​νϕ),Tμ​νEM=gα​β​Fα​μ​Fβ​ν−14​gμ​ν​Fα​β​Fα​β,Tμ​νϕ=Re⁡(Dμ​ϕ​Dν​ϕ¯)−12​gμ​ν​(Dα​ϕ​Dα​ϕ¯+m2​|ϕ|2),dF=0,d⋆F=⋆J,(Dμ​Dμ−m2)​ϕ=0.\displaystyle\begin{cases}\text{Ric}_{\mu\nu}(g)-\frac{1}{2}\text{R}(g)g_{\mu\nu}+\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}=2\left(T^{\text{EM}}_{\mu\nu}+T^{\phi}_{\mu\nu}\right),\\[3.00003pt] T^{\text{EM}}_{\mu\nu}=g^{\alpha\beta}F_{\alpha\mu}F_{\beta\nu}-\frac{1}{4}g_{\mu\nu}F^{\alpha\beta}F_{\alpha\beta},\\[3.00003pt] T^{\phi}_{\mu\nu}=\operatorname{Re}\left(D_{\mu}\phi\overline{D_{\nu}\phi}\right)-\frac{1}{2}g_{\mu\nu}\left(D_{\alpha}\phi\overline{D^{\alpha}\phi}+m^{2}|\phi|^{2}\right),\\[3.00003pt] dF=0,\quad d\star F=\star J,\\[3.00003pt] \left(D_{\mu}D^{\mu}-m^{2}\right)\phi=0.\end{cases}

The units are chosen so that c=4​π​G=ϵ0=1c=4\pi G=\epsilon_{0}=1 and the symbol ⋆\star denotes the Hodge-star operator. The charge generates an electromagnetic field which interacts with the spacetime itself and is modelled by the strength field tensor FF. The description of the charged scalar field through a complex-valued function and the use of the gauge covariant derivative

In the next sections, we are going to prove local well-posedness of a characteristic IVP for the first-order system (2.20)–(2.33). Solutions to such a system are elements (λCLOSE,(\lambda, ϖ,\varpi, θ,\theta, κ,\kappa, ϕ,\phi, Q,Q, r,r, ν,\nu, ζ,\zeta, OPENAu)A_{u}) in an appropriate Cartesian product of function spaces. The system is overdetermined, since we are solving 13 partial differential equations and an algebraic constraint for 10 unknowns. This is why we will solve for equations (2.21)-(2.22), (2.24)-(2.25), (2.27)-(2.30), (2.32) and we will consider equations (2.20), (2.23), (2.26), (2.31), (2.33) as constraints. In particular, for some U>0U>0, v0≥0v_{0}\geq 0, we will prescribe initial data on the set ([0,U]×{v0})∪({0}×[v0,+∞))⊂[0,U]×[0,+∞)\left([0,U]\times\{v_{0}\}\right)\cup\left(\{0\}\times[v_{0},+\infty)\right)\subset[0,U]\times[0,+\infty), seen as a subset of the conformal embedding of (𝒬,g𝒬)(\mathcal{Q},g_{\mathcal{Q}}) in (ℝ2,η)(\mathbb{R}^{2},\eta). In fact, we will specify:

{r⁡(u,v0),ζ⁡(u,v0),Au​(u,v0), for ​u∈[0,U],\begin{cases}r(u,v_{0}),\\ \zeta(u,v_{0}),\\ A_{u}(u,v_{0}),\end{cases}\quad\text{ for }u\in[0,U], (2.42)

and

{λ⁡(0,v),ϖ⁡(0,v),θ⁡(0,v),κ⁡(0,v),ϕ⁡(0,v),Q⁡(0,v), for v∈[v0,+∞).\begin{cases}\lambda(0,v),\\ \varpi(0,v),\\ \theta(0,v),\\ \kappa(0,v),\\ \phi(0,v),\\ Q(0,v),\end{cases}\quad\text{ for }v\in[v_{0},+\infty). (2.43)

The constraint equation (2.20) will be imposed on [0,U]×{v0}[0,U]\times\{v_{0}\} so that the function u↦ν⁡(u,v0)u\mapsto\nu(u,v_{0}) can be obtained from u↦r⁡(u,v0)u\mapsto r(u,v_{0}). In the following, we will denote the prescribed initial data by the zero subscript, e.g. r0​(u)≔r⁡(u,v0)r_{0}(u)\coloneqq r(u,v_{0}) and Au,0​(u)=Au​(u,v0)A_{u,0}(u)=A_{u}(u,v_{0}). The coordinates (u,v)(u,v) have not been fixed yet: we only required them to be null and to stem from the conformal embedding of section 2. We are going to fix a specific gauge in the following.

2.2 Assumptions

Let us make some general assumptions so that our spherically symmetric model describes a dynamical black hole asymptotically approaching (in some sense) a sub-extremal Reissner-Nordström solution with cosmological constant Λ\Lambda (we refer to [CG20, CF17, CGNS15a] for an overview of this spacetime). In this section, we fix the values v0v_{0} and UU so that v0≥0v_{0}\geq 0 and 0<U<+∞0<U<+\infty.

  • A)

    Gauge-fixing for the null coordinates: exploiting the diffeomorphism invariance of the Einstein-Maxwell-charged-Klein-Gordon system, we fix the uu coordinate by setting

    ν0​(u)=−1,∀u∈[0,U]\nu_{0}(u)=-1,\quad\forall\,u\in[0,U] (2.44)

    and we specify the vv coordinate by choosing

    κ0(v)=1,∀v∈[v0,+∞).\kappa_{0}(v)=1,\quad\forall\,v\in[v_{0},+\infty). (2.45)

    The negativity of ν0\nu_{0} can be related to the absence of anti-trapped surfaces. We also require the positivity of the area-radius:

    r0(u)>0∀u∈[0,U] and r(0,v)>0∀v∈[v0,+∞).r_{0}(u)>0\quad\forall\,u\in[0,U]\quad\text{ and }\quad r(0,v)>0\quad\forall\,v\in[v_{0},+\infty). (2.46)

Using the above gauge, we define

ℋ+≔{(u,v):u=0,v≥v0}\mathcal{H}^{+}\coloneqq\{(u,v)\colon\,u=0,v\geq v_{0}\}

as the event horizon of the dynamical black hole.

  • B)

    Regularity assumptions: we suppose that

    ν0,ζ0,λ0,θ0,κ0​ are ​C0​ functions in their respective domains,\nu_{0},\zeta_{0},\lambda_{0},\theta_{0},\kappa_{0}\text{ are }C^{0}\text{ functions in their respective domains},

    and that

    r0,ϖ0,ϕ0,Au,0,Q0​ are ​C1​ functions in their respective domains.r_{0},\varpi_{0},\phi_{0},A_{u,0},Q_{0}\text{ are }C^{1}\text{ functions in their respective domains}.

    We emphasize that θ0\theta_{0}, ζ0\zeta_{0} and ϕ0\phi_{0} are complex-valued functions. We will also make use of the function v↦r⁡(0,v)v\mapsto r(0,v), whose regularity depends on the regularity of λ0\lambda_{0}. These assumptions are enough to prove well-posedness of the first-order system. In order to demonstrate that such a system implies the Einstein-Maxwell equations, it is sufficient to additionally require that ν0\nu_{0}, λ0\lambda_{0} and κ0\kappa_{0} are C1C^{1} functions in their respective domains (see also the forthcoming remark 3.5).

  • C)

    Compatibility conditions: we require the following constraints to be satisfied:

    {r0′​(u)=ν0​(u),ϕ0′​(v)=θ0​(v)r⁡(0,v),ϖ0′​(v)=λ0​(v)2​m2​r​(0,v)2​|ϕ0​(v)|2+Q0​(v)​q​Im⁡(ϕ0​(v)​θ0¯​(v))+|θ0​(v)|22​κ0​(v),Q0′​(v)=q​r​(0,v)​Im⁡(ϕ0​(v)​θ0¯​(v))λ0​(v)=κ0​(v)​(1−2​ϖ0​(v)r⁡(0,v)+Q0​(v)2r​(0,v)2−Λ3​r​(0,v)2),\begin{cases}r^{\prime}_{0}(u)=\nu_{0}(u),\\ \phi^{\prime}_{0}(v)=\frac{\theta_{0}(v)}{r(0,v)},\\ \varpi^{\prime}_{0}(v)=\frac{\lambda_{0}(v)}{2}m^{2}r(0,v)^{2}|\phi_{0}(v)|^{2}+Q_{0}(v)q\operatorname{Im}(\phi_{0}(v)\overline{\theta_{0}}(v))+\frac{|\theta_{0}(v)|^{2}}{2\kappa_{0}(v)},\\ Q^{\prime}_{0}(v)=q\,r(0,v)\operatorname{Im}(\phi_{0}(v)\overline{\theta_{0}}(v))\\ \lambda_{0}(v)=\kappa_{0}(v)\left(1-\frac{2\varpi_{0}(v)}{r(0,v)}+\frac{Q_{0}(v)^{2}}{r(0,v)^{2}}-\frac{\Lambda}{3}r(0,v)^{2}\right),\end{cases} (2.47)

    for every u∈[0,U]u\in[0,U], every v∈[v0,+∞)v\in[v_{0},+\infty).

  • D)

    Absence of anti-trapped surfaces: we require

    ν(0,v)<0,∀v∈[v0,+∞).\nu(0,v)<0,\quad\forall\,v\in[v_{0},+\infty). (2.48)

    Once we construct a solution in a set 𝒟=[0,U′)×[v0,+∞)\mathcal{D}=[0,U^{\prime})\times[v_{0},+\infty) for 0<U′<+∞0<U^{\prime}<+\infty, the Raychaudhuri equation (2.6) implies that ν\nu remains negative in 𝒟\mathcal{D}.

Starting from section 5, we also assume the following.

  • E)

    Exponential Price law upper bound: we require that Λ>0\Lambda>0 and that, on the event horizon of the dynamical black hole, ϕ\phi decays as

    |ϕ|(0,v)+|∂vϕ|(0,v)≤Ce−s​v,∀v∈[v0,+∞)|\phi|(0,v)+|\partial_{v}\phi|(0,v)\leq Ce^{-sv},\quad\forall\,v\in[v_{0},+\infty) (2.49)

    for some C>0C>0, s>0s>0. This assumption is one of the main consequences of the presence of a positive cosmological constant Λ\Lambda. Here, the coordinate vv is related to an Eddington-Finkelstein coordinate adopted near the event horizon of a Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter black hole (see appendix B).

  • F)

    Asymptotically approaching a sub-extremal black hole: consider a fixed sub-extremal Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter spacetime. Let r+r_{+} and K+K_{+} be, respectively, the radius and the surface gravity of its event horizon, and let Q+Q_{+} be its charge and ϖ+\varpi_{+} its mass. Notice that several constraints apply on these four values, due to the sub-extremality condition.2727 27 Given K+≔12​∂r(1−μ)​(r+,ϖ+,Q+)K_{+}\coloneqq\frac{1}{2}\partial_{r}(1-\mu)(r_{+},\varpi_{+},Q_{+}), the values of ϖ+,Q+\varpi_{+},Q_{+} and r+r_{+} are constrained by the sub-extremality condition K+>0K_{+}>0 (see also [Hin18, section 3]). Moreover, (1−μ)​(r+,ϖ+,Q+)=0(1-\mu)(r_{+},\varpi_{+},Q_{+})=0. As in [CGNS15a], in the course of our work we assume that (1−μ)​(⋅,ϖ+,Q+)(1-\mu)(\cdot,\varpi_{+},Q_{+}) admits the three distinct and positive roots r−,r+r_{-},r_{+} and rCr_{C}, with r−<r+<rCr_{-}<r_{+}<r_{C}, corresponding to the radii of the Cauchy horizon, event horizon and cosmological horizon, respectively, of a Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter black hole. Then, on the event horizon, we require:2828 28 More generally, we could assign a condition on the lim sup\limsup of r,Q,ϖ,Kr,Q,\varpi,K. This requires minimal changes in the proof of proposition 5.2 and yields the same results.

    limv→+∞r⁡(0,v)\displaystyle\lim_{v\to+\infty}r(0,v) =r+,\displaystyle=r_{+}, (2.50)
    limv→+∞Q⁡(0,v)\displaystyle\lim_{v\to+\infty}Q(0,v) =Q+,\displaystyle=Q_{+}, (2.51)
    limv→+∞ϖ⁡(0,v)\displaystyle\lim_{v\to+\infty}\varpi(0,v) =ϖ+,\displaystyle=\varpi_{+}, (2.52)
    limv→+∞K⁡(0,v)\displaystyle\lim_{v\to+\infty}K(0,v) =K+.\displaystyle=K_{+}. (2.53)
  • G)

    Hawking’s area theorem: we assume2929 29 The case λ|ℋ+≡0\lambda_{|\mathcal{H}^{+}}\equiv 0 was studied in [CGNS15a, CGNS17], since Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter data were prescribed along ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+}. The case in which λ⁡(0,⋅)\lambda(0,\cdot) is identically zero for large values of the vv coordinate, but not for small ones, falls into that analysis after a coordinate shift. Moreover, due to our construction, the initial data along the event horizon are approaching the data of a Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter black hole in a non-trivial way. So, the apparent horizon does not coincide with the event horizon. By Hawking’s area theorem [CGNS18] and lemma 5.9, then, we are left to examine the case λ|ℋ+>0\lambda_{|\mathcal{H}^{+}}>0.

    λ⁡(0,v)>0,∀v≥v0.\lambda(0,v)>0,\quad\forall\,v\geq v_{0}. (2.54)

2.3 Notations and conventions

Given two non-negative functions ff and gg, we use the notation f≲gf\lesssim g to denote the existence of a positive constant CC such that f≤C​gf\leq Cg. The relation f≳gf\gtrsim g is defined analogously, and we write f∼gf\sim g whenever both f≲gf\lesssim g and f≳gf\gtrsim g hold. Constants denoted by the same letter may change from line to line. Whenever the symbols ≲\lesssim and ≳\gtrsim are used, we mean that the respective constants depend on the initial data only, except for the following cases:

  • •

    In the redshift region (section 5.3), constants depend on the initial data and possibly on the constant η\eta (see the statement of proposition 5.7),

  • •

    In the no-shift region (section 5.5), early blueshift region (sections 5.6 and 5.7) and late blueshift region (section 5.8), constants depend on the initial data, and possibly on η\eta, RR and YY (see propositions 5.7 and 5.12).

We often require quantities to be suitably large (or, analogously, sufficiently small), where this is meant with respect to the initial data and, possibly, with respect to other parameters. In the latter case, any additional dependence is specified.

3 Well-posedness of the initial value problem

Following [CGNS15], we are going to discuss local existence, uniqueness and continuous dependence with respect to the initial data for the solutions to the first-order system (2.20)-(2.33). In this section, we consider the constants U≥0U\geq 0 and V≥0V\geq 0, while we take v0=0v_{0}=0 for the sake of convenience. The initial data κ0\kappa_{0}, ν0\nu_{0} and Au,0A_{u,0} are taken to be constant, according to assumption (A) and (2.5). The case of more general functions ν0,κ0\nu_{0},\kappa_{0} and Au,0A_{u,0} follows in a straightforward way.

Definition 3.1 (solution to the PDE system)

We define a solution to the PDE system (2.20)–(2.32), with initial conditions (2.42), (2.43) and satisfying the regularity assumptions (B) and constraint (2.33), to be a vector (λ𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸,(\lambda, ϖ,\varpi, θ,\theta, κ,\kappa, ϕ,\phi, Q,Q, r,r, ν,\nu, ζ,\zeta, 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁Au)A_{u}) of continuous functions defined on [0,U]×[0,V][0,U]\times[0,V], such that all partial derivatives appearing in such a system are continuous.

Theorem 3.2 (local existence and uniqueness)

Under the assumptions (A), (B), (C) and (D), let us prescribe initial data on the characteristic initial set [0,U]×{0}∪{0}×[0,V][0,U]\times\{0\}\cup\{0\}\times[0,V] for some 0<U<+∞0<U<+\infty and 0<V<+∞0<V<+\infty. We define the quantity

N0≔\displaystyle N_{0}\coloneqq (‖λ0‖+‖ϖ0‖+‖θ0‖+‖κ0​‖+‖ϕ0‖+‖​Q0‖)L∞​([0,V])\displaystyle\left(\|\lambda_{0}\|+\|\varpi_{0}\|+\|\theta_{0}\|+\|\kappa_{0}\|+\|\phi_{0}\|+\|Q_{0}\|\right)_{L^{\infty}([0,V])}
+(‖r0‖+‖ν0‖+‖ζ0‖+‖Au,0‖)L∞​([0,U]).\displaystyle+\left(\|r_{0}\|+\|\nu_{0}\|+\|\zeta_{0}\|+\|A_{u,0}\|\right)_{L^{\infty}([0,U])}.

Then, there exists a time of existence 0<ϵ=ϵ⁡(N0)≤U0<\epsilon=\epsilon(N_{0})\leq U for which the characteristic IVP for the first-order system (2.20)–(2.33) admits a unique solution in 𝒟ϵ≔[0,ϵ]×[0,V]\mathcal{D}_{\epsilon}\coloneqq[0,\epsilon]\times[0,V], the solution being such that the functions r,νr,\nu and κ\kappa are bounded away from zero in 𝒟ϵ\mathcal{D}_{\epsilon}.

Similarly, there exists a time of existence 0<ϵ=ϵ⁡(N0)≤V0<\epsilon=\epsilon(N_{0})\leq V such that the characteristic IVP admits a unique solution in 𝒟ϵ≔[0,U]×[0,ϵ]\mathcal{D}^{\epsilon}\coloneqq[0,U]\times[0,\epsilon] and such that the functions r,νr,\nu and κ\kappa are bounded away from zero in 𝒟ϵ\mathcal{D}^{\epsilon}.

Proof.

Local existence can be proved via a fixed-point argument. Given VV, where 0<V<+∞0<V<+\infty, let us choose ϵ>0\epsilon>0 small enough, whose value will ultimately depend on N0N_{0}. Let us then consider the metric space

Sϵ≔\displaystyle S_{\epsilon}\coloneqq BRλ(λ0)×BRϖ(ϖ0)×BRθ(θ0)×BRκ(1)×BRϕ(ϕ0)×\displaystyle B_{R_{\lambda}}(\lambda_{0})\times B_{R_{\varpi}}(\varpi_{0})\times B_{R_{\theta}}(\theta_{0})\times B_{R_{\kappa}}(1)\times B_{R_{\phi}}(\phi_{0})\times
BRQ​(Q0)×I⁡(α,β,r0)×BRν​(−1)×BRζ​(ζ0)×BRA​(0),\displaystyle B_{R_{Q}}(Q_{0})\times I(\alpha,\beta,r_{0})\times B_{R_{\nu}}(-1)\times B_{R_{\zeta}}(\zeta_{0})\times B_{R_{A}}(0),

endowed with the L∞L^{\infty} norm, where

BRλ​(λ0)≔{λ∈C0​(𝒟ϵ,ℝ):‖λ⁡(u,v)−λ0​(v)‖L∞​(𝒟ϵ)≤Rλ}B_{R_{\lambda}}(\lambda_{0})\coloneqq\{\lambda\in C^{0}(\mathcal{D}_{\epsilon};\mathbb{R})\colon\,\|\lambda(u,v)-\lambda_{0}(v)\|_{L^{\infty}(\mathcal{D}_{\epsilon})}\leq R_{\lambda}\}

for Rλ>0R_{\lambda}>0 and

3. The constraints propagate along the evolution: first, we know that constraint (2.20) holds at v=0v=0. To prove its validity in 𝒟ϵ\mathcal{D}_{\epsilon}, it is enough to show that

The latter can be shown to be zero by using basic properties of complex numbers, such as ∂u(|θ|2)=2​Re⁡(θ¯​∂uθ)\partial_{u}\left(|\theta|^{2}\right)=2\operatorname{Re}\left(\overline{\theta}\partial_{u}\theta\right) and ∂v(|ζ|2)=2​Re⁡(ζ¯​∂vζ)\partial_{v}\left(|\zeta|^{2}\right)=2\operatorname{Re}\left(\overline{\zeta}\partial_{v}\zeta\right), jointly with (2.27) and (2.28).
Final remarks: The fixed-point theorem only shows uniqueness of the solution in SϵS_{\epsilon}. To prove uniqueness in the general setting, we consider two solutions f1f_{1} and f2f_{2} having same initial data. Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} be the intersection of their domains of existence. If we take a point (u,v)(u,v) in 𝒟\mathcal{D}, we can consider the initial value problem with data prescribed on [0,u]×{0}[0,u]\times\{0\} ∪\cup {0}×[0,v]\{0\}\times[0,v]. By the local existence result in SϵS_{\epsilon}, there exists a unique solution f3f_{3} in ℰ≔[0,ϵ1]×[0,v]\mathcal{E}\coloneqq[0,\epsilon_{1}]\times[0,v] for some ϵ1>0\epsilon_{1}>0 small, with ϵ1\epsilon_{1} depending on the norm of the initial data N0N_{0}. Since the solution is unique, it must be that f1≡f3≡f2f_{1}\equiv f_{3}\equiv f_{2} on ℰ\mathcal{E}.

We can repeat the procedure by considering the initial value problem with initial data in [ϵ1,2​ϵ1]×{0}[\epsilon_{1},2\epsilon_{1}]\times\{0\} ∪\cup {ϵ1}×[0,v]\{\epsilon_{1}\}\times[0,v]. These initial data are again controlled by N0N_{0}, since the L∞L^{\infty} norm of f1≡f2≡f3f_{1}\equiv f_{2}\equiv f_{3} in [0,ϵ1]×[0,v][0,\epsilon_{1}]\times[0,v] is itself controlled by N0N_{0}. So, we obtain a further stripe of size ϵ1\epsilon_{1} on which f1≡f2f_{1}\equiv f_{2}. We can iterate this procedure by subdividing the entire set 𝒟\mathcal{D} into stripes of side ϵ1\epsilon_{1}. ∎

Remark 3.3 (maximal past sets)

A set 𝒫⊂[0,U]×[v0,+∞)\mathcal{P}\subset[0,U]\times[v_{0},+\infty) is a past set if [0,u]×[v0,v]⊂𝒫[0,u]\times[v_{0},v]\subset\mathcal{P} for every (u,v)∈𝒫(u,v)\in\mathcal{P}. As noticed in [CGNS15, Theorem 4.4], every solution to the characteristic IVP with initial data prescribed on [0,U]×[v0,+∞)[0,U]\times[v_{0},+\infty), for some v0≥0v_{0}\geq 0, and satisfying assumptions (A), (B), (C) and (D), can be extended to a maximal past set 𝒫⊃[0,U]×{v0}∪{0}×[v0,+∞)\mathcal{P}\supset[0,U]\times\{v_{0}\}\cup\{0\}\times[v_{0},+\infty).

Remark 3.5 (On the equivalence between the first-order and second-order system)

Under assumptions (A), (B), (C), (D), the second-order system (2.6)–(2.10), (2.30)–(2.31) implies the first-order system (2.20)–(2.33).

On the other hand, if (r,Ω2,ϕ,Q)(r,\Omega^{2},\phi,Q) solves the second-order system (namely rr, Ω2\Omega^{2}, ϕ\phi, QQ satisfy the system, they are continuous functions and all derivatives in the second-order system are continuous), then the Raychaudhuri equations and the wave equation for rr imply that r∈C2r\in C^{2}. Such a property is guaranteed for a solution to the first-order system if we additionally require that

(B2) ​ν0,λ0​ and ​κ0​ are ​C1​ functions in their respective domains.\textbf{(B2) }\nu_{0},\lambda_{0}\text{ and }\kappa_{0}\text{ are }C^{1}\text{ functions in their respective domains.}

A straightforward adaptation of [CGNS15, Section 6] reveals that assumption (B2) is in fact sufficient to show that a solution to the first-order system solves the second-order system, in the above-mentioned sense.

Therefore, we say that the first-order system and the second-order system are equivalent if assumptions (A), (B), (B2), (C) and (D) are satisfied.

Remark 3.6 (general properties of solutions)

As a consequence of (3.1)-(3.10), we have that, for a solution f=(λ𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸,f=(\lambda, ϖ,\varpi, θ,\theta, κ,\kappa, ϕ,\phi, Q,Q, r,r, ν,\nu, ζ,\zeta, 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁Au)A_{u}) of the first order system in a past set 𝒫\mathcal{P}:

    κ\kappa is positive,

  • •

    ν\nu is negative.

We notice that the renormalized Hawking mass ϖ\varpi is generally not a monotonic function, differently from the case of the Einstein-Maxwell-(real) scalar field system. However, we have

∂u(ϖ−Q22​r)<0 and ∂v(ϖ−Q22​r)≥0\partial_{u}\left(\varpi-\frac{Q^{2}}{2r}\right)<0\quad\text{ and }\quad\partial_{v}\left(\varpi-\frac{Q^{2}}{2r}\right)\geq 0

in the region {(u,v):λ⁡(u,v)≥0}\{(u,v)\colon\,\lambda(u,v)\geq 0\}.

4 The extension criterion

We are now interested in conditions that let us extend the domain of existence of a solution to the characteristic IVP. Results of this sort were obtained in [Daf05], [CGNS15] and [Kom13]. In [Daf05, Kom13], in particular, the lack of extensions was used to characterize the first singularities possibly present in the considered spacetimes, therefore addressing that problem of spacetime predictability which, in more general settings, is captured by the weak cosmic censorship conjecture. In particular, the following result was proved in [Kom13] for the Einstein-Maxwell-(charged) scalar field system with Λ=0\Lambda=0: given initial data prescribed on [0,U]×{0}∪{0}×[0,V][0,U]\times\{0\}\cup\{0\}\times[0,V] for some U,V∈ℝ0+U,V\in\mathbb{R}_{0}^{+}, where the initial data satisfy the assumptions of the local existence theorem 3.2, a solution ff defined in

𝒟≔[0,U′)×[0,V′),\mathcal{D}\coloneqq[0,U^{\prime})\times[0,V^{\prime}),

with 0<U′<U0<U^{\prime}<U and 0<V′<V0<V^{\prime}<V, can be extended along both the future ingoing and outgoing directions if we can control the L∞L^{\infty} norm of the solution and of the inverse of rr and Ω2\Omega^{2}. In [Kom13], it was also shown that for this to happen, two conditions are sufficient: that the area-radius function can be estimated in 𝒟\mathcal{D} from below and above by positive constants, and that the spacetime volume of 𝒟\mathcal{D}, i.e.

∫𝒟Ω2​𝑑u​𝑑v\int_{\mathcal{D}}\Omega^{2}dudv

is bounded from above. The results of [Kom13] apply to our setting, where the cosmological constant is possibly non-zero, since the presence of Λ\Lambda in (2.8) does not require any substantial change in the proofs of the above statements.

The main part of the proof of the extension criterion in [Kom13] consists of bounding the quantity

∬𝒟r2​Tu​v∼∫0V′∫0U′|ν|​κ​(m2​r2​|ϕ|2+Q2r2)​𝑑u​𝑑v\iint_{\mathcal{D}}r^{2}T_{uv}\sim\int_{0}^{V^{\prime}}\int_{0}^{U^{\prime}}|\nu|\kappa\left(m^{2}r^{2}|\phi|^{2}+\frac{Q^{2}}{r^{2}}\right)dudv (4.1)

in order to obtain estimates on the spacetime integrals of several PDE variables. This allows to get a bound on ϕ\phi when integrating the Klein-Gordon equation (2.10):

∂u∂vϕ=−1r​(Du​r​∂vϕ+∂vr​Du​ϕ)+i​q​Q​Ω24​r2​ϕ−m2​Ω24​ϕ.\partial_{u}{\partial_{v}{\phi}}=-\frac{1}{r}\left(D_{u}{r}\partial_{v}{\phi}+\partial_{v}{r}D_{u}{\phi}\right)+\frac{iqQ\Omega^{2}}{4r^{2}}\phi-\frac{m^{2}\Omega^{2}}{4}\phi.

As a final step, the bound on ϕ\phi is applied to obtain the remaining uniform bounds. This proof requires a bootstrap argument, due to the need to bound ϕ\phi also at the right hand side of (2.10). Such an argument can be closed after partitioning 𝒟\mathcal{D} in ϵ\epsilon-small rectangles.

On the other hand, the expressions (3.1)–(3.10) satisfied by the solution to the characteristic IVP suggest that it might be sufficient to uniformly bound the iterated integrals3232 32 As we will see, it is enough to bound just the iterated integral taken with respect to the vv variable, using the good signs of the charge function and scalar field terms at the right hand side of (3.8). in (4.1) to estimate the remaining PDE variables. We present here a proof that uses this insight. In particular, we demonstrate that an extension result for the first-order system follows from the requirement of an upper and lower bound for the function rr,3333 33 This was also the case for the real, massless scalar field system analysed in [Daf05a] (Λ=0\Lambda=0) and in [CGNS15] (for any value of Λ\Lambda), where monotonicity properties were exploited. In our case, the same properties do not generally hold. without adopting any bootstrap method and essentially only using the positivity of Tu​vT_{uv}. We stress that, with respect to the extension criterion for the second-order system, slightly less regularity is required: the initial data ν0,λ0\nu_{0},\lambda_{0} and κ0\kappa_{0} only need to be C0C^{0} in their respective domains (see remark 3.5).

|ζ|​(u,v)≤C+C​∫0u∫0v|ζ​λ|r​(u′,v′)​d​v′​d​u′+C​∫0u∫0v|ν|​κr​|ϕ|​(m2​r2+|q​Q|)​(u′,v′)​d​v′​d​u′,|\zeta|(u,v)\leq C+C\int_{0}^{u}\int_{0}^{v}\frac{|\zeta\lambda|}{r}(u^{\prime},v^{\prime})dv^{\prime}du^{\prime}+C\int_{0}^{u}\int_{0}^{v}\frac{|\nu|\kappa}{r}|\phi|\left(m^{2}r^{2}+|qQ|\right)(u^{\prime},v^{\prime})dv^{\prime}du^{\prime},

where the order of integration could be reversed due to Fubini-Tonelli’s theorem. The last integral can be bounded using (4.6) and (4.10). Moreover, we define

ζϵ​(u)≔maxv∈[0,V′−ϵ]⁡|ζ|​(u,v),\zeta_{\epsilon}(u)\coloneqq\max_{v\in[0,V^{\prime}-\epsilon]}|\zeta|(u,v),

for every u∈[0,U′)u\in[0,U^{\prime}) and for some fixed 0<ϵ<V′0<\epsilon<V^{\prime}. Therefore, the previous lines give

ζϵ​(u)≤C+C​∫0uζϵ​(u′)​(∫0V′−ϵ|λ|​(u′,v′)​d​v′)​d​u′.\zeta_{\epsilon}(u)\leq C+C\int_{0}^{u}\zeta_{\epsilon}(u^{\prime})\left(\int_{0}^{V^{\prime}-\epsilon}|\lambda|(u^{\prime},v^{\prime})dv^{\prime}\right)du^{\prime}. (4.11)

We now use (4.4) in (4.11) to obtain

ζϵ​(u)≤C⁡(1+∫0uζϵ​(u′)​d​u′).\zeta_{\epsilon}(u)\leq C\left(1+\int_{0}^{u}\zeta_{\epsilon}(u^{\prime})du^{\prime}\right).

By applying Grönwall’s inequality, and then taking the limit ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0, we finally get a uniform bound on ζ\zeta.
Uniform bound on |ϕ|\bm{|\phi|}: equation (3.5), together with the uniform bounds on AuA_{u}, ζ\zeta and rr, gives

|ϕ|​(u,v)≤supv∈[0,V′)|ϕ0|​(v)+∫0u|ζ|r​(u′,v)​d​u′≤C,|\phi|(u,v)\leq\sup_{v\in[0,V^{\prime})}|\phi_{0}|(v)+\int_{0}^{u}\frac{|\zeta|}{r}(u^{\prime},v)du^{\prime}\leq C,

where CC does not depend on the value of u∈[0,U′)u\in[0,U^{\prime}).
Uniform bound on |Q|\bm{|Q|}: equation (3.6), together with the uniform bounds on rr, ϕ\phi and ζ\zeta, gives

|Q|​(u,v)≤supv∈[0,V′)|Q0|​(v)+|q|​∫0u(r​|ϕ|​|ζ|)​(u′,v)​d​u′≤C,|Q|(u,v)\leq\sup_{v\in[0,V^{\prime})}|Q_{0}|(v)+|q|\int_{0}^{u}\left(r|\phi||\zeta|\right)(u^{\prime},v)du^{\prime}\leq C,

for every vv in [0,V′)[0,V^{\prime}).
Uniform (lower) bound on |ν|\bm{|\nu|}: the above uniform bounds on ϕ\phi and QQ are sufficient to prove that ν\nu is bounded away from zero in 𝒟\mathcal{D}, as can be seen from the finiteness of the integrals in expression (4.5).
Uniform (lower) bound on κ\bm{\kappa}: the estimates on ζ\zeta, ν\nu and rr can be applied to (3.4) to bound κ\kappa away from zero.
Remaining uniform bounds: a bound on λ\lambda follows after integrating (2.37) in uu and noticing that every term at the right hand side of the equation is uniformly bounded. The previous estimate on λ\lambda can be applied to (4.8) to get a uniform bound on θ\theta, since we have estimated each function appearing in the integrand terms of (4.8) in the sup𝒟\sup_{\mathcal{D}}-norm. Finally, we can divide both sides of (2.36) by κ\kappa to bound ϖ\varpi uniformly, due to the estimates from above that we have for QQ, rr, λ\lambda, and to the estimates from below that we have for κ\kappa and rr.
2. Construction of the extension: let δ,ϵ>0\delta,\epsilon>0 be small and consider the initial value problem with initial data prescribed on

[0,U′−ϵ]×{V′−δ}∪{0}×[V′−δ,V′+δ].[0,U^{\prime}-\epsilon]\times\{V^{\prime}-\delta\}\cup\{0\}\times[V^{\prime}-\delta,V^{\prime}+\delta].

By the local existence theorem 3.2, and due to the uniform bound on N⁡(𝒟)N(\mathcal{D}) proved in the previous steps, there exists a minimum time of existence δ~>0\tilde{\delta}>0, whose size depends only on N0N_{0}, such that we can construct a solution to our PDE system in 𝒟1≔[0,U′−ϵ]×[V′−δ,V′−δ+δ~]\mathcal{D}_{1}\coloneqq[0,U^{\prime}-\epsilon]\times[V^{\prime}-\delta,V^{\prime}-\delta+\tilde{\delta}]. Since we chose the minimum time of existence, this result holds whenever we translate the initial null segments along the vv–direction, provided that the ingoing segment stays in 𝒟\mathcal{D} and that the outgoing segment is contained in {0}×[0,V]\{0\}\times[0,V]. Without loss of generality, we therefore consider the new shifted rectangle to be 𝒟1≔[0,U′−ϵ]×[V′−δ,V′+δ]\mathcal{D}_{1}\coloneqq\left[0,U^{\prime}-\epsilon\right]\times[V^{\prime}-\delta,V^{\prime}+\delta], where the value of δ\delta is possibly different from the original one, and take ϵ=δ2\epsilon=\frac{\delta}{2}.

The same construction can be followed with respect to the initial data prescribed on

[U′−δ,U′+δ]×{0}∪{U′−δ}×[0,V′−δ2].[U^{\prime}-\delta,U^{\prime}+\delta]\times\{0\}\cup\{U^{\prime}-\delta\}\times\left[0,V^{\prime}-\frac{\delta}{2}\right].

In particular, we define 𝒟2≔[U′−δ,U′+δ]×[0,V′−δ2]\mathcal{D}_{2}\coloneqq[U^{\prime}-\delta,U^{\prime}+\delta]\times[0,V^{\prime}-\frac{\delta}{2}], for the same value of δ\delta (if a smaller value of δ\delta is required by the local existence theorem, we repeat the construction of 𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1} and 𝒟2\mathcal{D}_{2} from scratch, starting from the ingoing null segment).

We now consider the point p=(U′−δ2,V′−δ2)p=\left(U^{\prime}-\frac{\delta}{2},V^{\prime}-\frac{\delta}{2}\right). By performing a coordinate shift, we can set p=(0,0)p=(0,0). We then construct a solution from the initial data prescribed on [0,32​δ]×{0}∪{0}×[0,32​δ]\left[0,\frac{3}{2}\delta\right]\times\{0\}\cup\{0\}\times\left[0,\frac{3}{2}\delta\right]. By the proof of theorem 3.2, the L∞L^{\infty} norm of the (continuous) solution in the compact sets 𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1} and 𝒟2\mathcal{D}_{2} is controlled by N0N_{0}. Therefore, for the initial value problem prescribed on these null segments, the minimum time of existence of solutions is again given by the previously obtained δ\delta. Thus, we obtain a continuous solution in

𝒟3≔[0,δ]×[0,32​δ],\mathcal{D}_{3}\coloneqq[0,\delta]\times\left[0,\frac{3}{2}\delta\right],

which is enough to conclude the proof. ∎

Remark 4.2 (A counter-example)

Let us consider a solution to the first-order system defined, modulo the S​O​(3)SO(3) orbit space, in a half-open rectangle in the Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter spacetime. Assume that the rectangle lies in the outer domain of communications, where one of the corners of the closure of the rectangle coincides with i+i^{+}.

Although the area-radius function is bounded in such a rectangle, no extensions are possible due to the singularity originating at i+i^{+}. The reason for this is that assumption (D) does not hold and so theorem 4.1 does not apply: ν\nu vanishes along the cosmological horizon and thus the L∞L^{\infty} norm of ν−1\nu^{-1} is unbounded along the initial outgoing null segment. In particular, we do not have a lower bound on the time of existence when constructing local solutions.

5 Existence and stability of the Cauchy horizon

We recall that a set 𝒫⊂[0,U]×[v0,+∞)\mathcal{P}\subset[0,U]\times[v_{0},+\infty) is called a past set if J−​(u,v)≔[0,u]×[v0,v]J^{-}(u,v)\coloneqq[0,u]\times[v_{0},v] is contained in 𝒫\mathcal{P} for every (u,v)(u,v) in 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Given a set S⊂[0,U]×[v0,+∞)S\subset[0,U]\times[v_{0},+\infty), we define

J−​(S)≔⋃(u,v)∈SJ−​(u,v),J^{-}(S)\coloneqq\bigcup_{(u,v)\in S}J^{-}(u,v),

and analogous definitions hold for J+​(S)J^{+}(S), I−​(S)I^{-}(S) and I+​(S)I^{+}(S) (where I−​(u,v)≔[0,u)×[v0,v)I^{-}(u,v)\coloneqq[0,u)\times[v_{0},v)).

In the following, we work with a solution to the characteristic IVP of section 2.1, defined in the maximal past set 𝒫\mathcal{P} containing

𝒟0≔[0,U]×{v0}∪{0}×[v0,+∞), for some 0<U<+∞,v0≥0.\mathcal{D}_{0}\coloneqq[0,U]\times\{v_{0}\}\cup\{0\}\times[v_{0},+\infty),\quad\text{ for some }0<U<+\infty,\,v_{0}\geq 0.

The existence of 𝒫\mathcal{P} is guaranteed by the well-posedness results proved in section 3. In turn, its maximality is to be interpreted in the sense that the solution cannot be defined on any larger past set (see also theorem 4.1). From now on, we suppose that assumptions (A), (B), (B2) (see remark 3.5), (C), (D), (E), (F) and (G) hold. In particular, we are going to use the equations from both the first-order and second-order systems, depending on the most convenient choice.

In this context, 𝒫\mathcal{P} corresponds to a region containing the event horizon and extending inside the dynamical black hole under investigation. In the course of the following proofs, we actually work with solutions defined in

𝒫∩{v≥v1},\mathcal{P}\cap\{v\geq v_{1}\},

for some v1≥v0v_{1}\geq v_{0}. We require (finitely many times) that the values of UU and v1v_{1} are, respectively, sufficiently small and sufficiently large. A posteriori, this implies that our results hold in a region adjacent to both the event horizon and the Cauchy horizon of the dynamical black hole under investigation. Notice, however, that we do not modify the initial data set 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0} during the proof by bootstrap. We only highlight the steps where we constrain the values of UU and v1v_{1}. This occurs finitely many times and depends only on the L∞L^{\infty} norm of the initial data and possibly on η\eta, RR (see proposition 5.7), YY (see proposition 5.12), and ε\varepsilon (see proposition 5.13). These quantities can ultimately be chosen in terms of the initial data.

In this section, we are also going to prove that the apparent horizon

𝒜≔{(u,v)∈[0,U]×[v0,+∞):λ(u,v)=0}\mathcal{A}\coloneqq\{(u,v)\in[0,U]\times[v_{0},+\infty)\colon\,\lambda(u,v)=0\}

is a non-empty C1C^{1} curve for large values of the vv coordinate. It is also convenient to define the regular region

ℛ≔{(u,v)∈[0,U]×[v0,+∞):λ(u,v)>0},\mathcal{R}\coloneqq\{(u,v)\in[0,U]\times[v_{0},+\infty)\colon\,\lambda(u,v)>0\},

which, as we will see, extends from the event horizon to part of the redshift region. The remaining part of the black hole interior is occupied by the trapped region

𝒯≔{(u,v)∈[0,U]×[v0,+∞):λ(u,v)<0}.\mathcal{T}\coloneqq\{(u,v)\in[0,U]\times[v_{0},+\infty)\colon\,\lambda(u,v)<0\}. (5.1)

For the system under analysis, the regular region is a priori non-empty, differently from the case of the Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter solution. In the latter case, indeed, every 2-sphere in the interior of the black hole region is a trapped surface and, furthermore, the apparent horizon coincides with the event horizon.

Remark 5.1 (on the main constants)

Throughout the bootstrap procedure, we use the following auxiliary, positive quantities:

  • •

    Redshift region (proposition 5.7): η\eta, δ=δ⁡(η,β)\delta=\delta(\eta,\beta), R=R⁡(δ)R=R(\delta),

  • •

    No-shift region (proposition 5.12): ε=ε⁡(β)\varepsilon=\varepsilon(\beta), Δ=Δ⁡(ε)\Delta=\Delta(\varepsilon), Y=Y⁡(Δ)Y=Y(\Delta),

  • •

    Early blueshift region (see (5.117)): β\beta.

These constants can be ultimately defined in terms of the initial data.

In particular, the following constraints will be required:

  • •

    In lemma 5.17, δ\delta and ε\varepsilon are required small with respect to β\beta, in such a way that

    K−K+​β>α⁡(δ,ε),\frac{K_{-}}{K_{+}}\beta>\alpha(\delta,\varepsilon),

    where 0<α≲δ+ε0<\alpha\lesssim\delta+\varepsilon,

  • •

    In proposition 5.7, we require 0<δ<η0<\delta<\eta and 0<r+−R<δ0<r_{+}-R<\delta to be satisfied,

  • •

    In proposition 5.13, we take Δ∈(0,ε)\Delta\in(0,\varepsilon) and YY such that 0<Y−r−<Δ0<Y-r_{-}<\Delta.

5.1 Event horizon

Recall that ϖ+\varpi_{+}, Q+Q_{+} and Λ\Lambda are the parameters of the final sub-extremal Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter black hole (see assumption (F)), while r+r_{+} and K+K_{+} denote the radius and the surface gravity, respectively, associated to its event horizon.

For every v≥v0v\geq v_{0}, we have:

0<r+−r⁡(0,v)≤Cℋ​e−2​s​v,\displaystyle 0<r_{+}-r(0,v)\leq C_{\mathcal{H}}e^{-2sv}, (5.2)
0<λ⁡(0,v)≤Cℋ​e−2​s​v,\displaystyle 0<\lambda(0,v)\leq C_{\mathcal{H}}e^{-2sv}, (5.3)

|Q⁡(0,v)−Q+|≤Cℋ​e−2​s​v,\displaystyle|Q(0,v)-Q_{+}|\leq C_{\mathcal{H}}e^{-2sv}, (5.6)

|Du​ϕ|​(0,v)≤{Cℋ​|ν|​(0,v)​e−s​v,if​s<2​K+,Cℋ​(v−v0),if​s=2​K+,Cℋ,if​s>2​K+,\displaystyle|D_{u}\phi|(0,v)\leq\begin{cases}C_{\mathcal{H}}|\nu|(0,v)e^{-sv},&\mathrm{if}\,\,s<2K_{+},\\ C_{\mathcal{H}}(v-v_{0}),&\mathrm{if}\,\,s=2K_{+},\\ C_{\mathcal{H}},&\mathrm{if}\,\,s>2K_{+},\end{cases} (5.9)
|ϕ|​(0,v)+|∂vϕ|​(0,v)≤Cℋ​e−s​v.\displaystyle|\phi|(0,v)+|\partial_{v}\phi|(0,v)\leq C_{\mathcal{H}}e^{-sv}. (5.10)

where CℋC_{\mathcal{H}} is a positive constant depending only on the initial data.

In the following, the letter CC will denote a positive constant depending uniquely on the initial data. Moreover, we will exploit the assumptions (2.45) and (2.48) on κ\kappa and ν\nu, respectively, multiple times in the next computations.

and so, by integrating and due to (2.44):

|limz→+∞λν​(0,z)|≤(C​e−(2​K++2​s−ϵ)​v+|λ|​(0,v)​e−(2​K+−ϵ)​v)​e(2​K+−ϵ)​v1,\left|\lim_{z\to+\infty}\frac{\lambda}{\nu}(0,z)\right|\leq\left(Ce^{-(2K_{+}+2s-\epsilon)v}+|\lambda|(0,v)e^{-(2K_{+}-\epsilon)v}\right)e^{(2K_{+}-\epsilon)v_{1}},

limz→+∞λν​(0,z)=0.\lim_{z\to+\infty}\frac{\lambda}{\nu}(0,z)=0. (5.17)

|Q⁡(0,v)−Q+|=C​|∫v+∞r2​(0,v′)​Im⁡(ϕ​∂vϕ¯)​(0,v′)​d​v′|≤C​e−2​s​v,∀v≥v0.\left|Q(0,v)-Q_{+}\right|=C\left|\int_{v}^{+\infty}r^{2}(0,v^{\prime})\operatorname{Im}(\phi\overline{\partial_{v}\phi})(0,v^{\prime})dv^{\prime}\right|\leq Ce^{-2sv},\quad\forall\,v\geq v_{0}. (5.18)

In order to bound the renormalized Hawking mass, we first notice that (2.49) and (5.11) give:

0\displaystyle 0 <λ⁡(0,v)=ν⁡(0,v)​∫+∞v∂v(λν)​(0,v′)​d​v′\displaystyle<\lambda(0,v)=\nu(0,v)\int_{+\infty}^{v}\partial_{v}\left(\frac{\lambda}{\nu}\right)(0,v^{\prime})dv^{\prime}

≤C​|ν|​(0,v)​e−2​s​v​∫v+∞∂v(1ν)​(0,v′)​d​v′=C​e−2​s​v,\displaystyle\leq C|\nu|(0,v)e^{-2sv}\int_{v}^{+\infty}\partial_{v}\left(\frac{1}{\nu}\right)(0,v^{\prime})dv^{\prime}=Ce^{-2sv}, (5.20)

0<r+−r⁡(0,v)≤C​e−2​s​v.0<r_{+}-r(0,v)\leq Ce^{-2sv}.

Due to definition (2.34) and to the decays proved for QQ and ϖ\varpi, this is also sufficient to prove

This result also allows us to improve (5.13) and, after following the same steps leading to (5.14) and (5.15), to obtain:

|ν|​(0,v)∼e2​K+​(v−v0),∀v≥v0.|\nu|(0,v)\sim e^{2K_{+}(v-v_{0})},\quad\forall\,v\geq v_{0}. (5.22)

Finally, (5.10) follows from (2.49). We then choose CℋC_{\mathcal{H}} as the largest of the previous positive constants depending on the initial data. ∎

Remark 5.3 (Redshift effect)

From the point of view of a family of observers crossing the event horizon ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+}, the energy associated to the null geodesics ruling ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+} decays as e−2​K+​ve^{-2K_{+}v} due to the redshift effect.

This is the same rate at which we found the geometric quantity |ν−1​Du​ϕ|\left|\nu^{-1}D_{u}\phi\right| to decay for s>2​K+s>2K_{+} along the event horizon (see (5.9)). Here, the constant ss is the same as in (2.49). For s<2​K+s<2K_{+}, the quantity |ν−1​Du​ϕ|\left|\nu^{-1}D_{u}\phi\right| decays as e−s​ve^{-sv} or faster, which is the same rate dictated by the Price law upper bound (2.49). From these two different rates, we deduce the physical relevance of two competing phenomena along the event horizon: the redshift effect and the decay of the scalar field ϕ\phi.

5.2 Level sets of the area-radius function

The strategy of the next proofs consists of partitioning the past set 𝒫\mathcal{P}. In the two-dimensional quotient space that we are considering, such subsets are mainly separated by curves where the area-radius function is constant. We then proceed by analysing the sets

Γϱ≔{(u,v)∈𝒫:r⁡(u,v)=ϱ}\Gamma_{\varrho}\coloneqq\{(u,v)\in\mathcal{P}\,\colon\,r(u,v)=\varrho\} (5.25)

for some ϱ∈(0,r+)\varrho\in(0,r_{+}).

Lemma 5.4 (properties of Γϱ\Gamma_{\varrho})

Assume that Γϱ≠∅\Gamma_{\varrho}\neq\varnothing. Then, the following set equality holds:

Γϱ={(uϱ(v),v):v∈[v1,+∞)},\Gamma_{\varrho}=\{(u_{\varrho}(v),v)\,\colon\,v\in[v_{1},+\infty)\},

for some v1≥v0v_{1}\geq v_{0} and for some C1C^{1} function uϱ:[v1,+∞)→ℝu_{\varrho}\colon[v_{1},+\infty)\to\mathbb{R} such that r⁡(uϱ​(⋅),⋅)≡ϱr(u_{\varrho}(\cdot),\cdot)\equiv\varrho. Moreover, let

v¯≔inf{v≥v1:λ⁡(uϱ​(v),v)≤0}.\underline{v}\coloneqq\inf\{v\geq v_{1}\colon\lambda(u_{\varrho}(v),v)\leq 0\}. (5.26)

Then, the following properties are satisfied:

   𝐏​𝚪​𝟐.\bm{\mathrm{P}\Gamma 2.}

uϱ′​(v)=−λ​(uϱ​(v),v)ν​(uϱ​(v),v),u^{\prime}_{\varrho}(v)=-\frac{\lambda(u_{\varrho}(v),v)}{\nu(u_{\varrho}(v),v)}, (5.27)
   𝐏​𝚪​𝟑.\bm{\mathrm{P}\Gamma 3.}

λ⁡(uϱ​(v),v)≤0\lambda(u_{\varrho}(v),v)\leq 0 for every v≥v¯v\geq\underline{v}.

The existence of such a uϱu_{\varrho} follows from the implicit function theorem, together with the fact that ν<0\nu<0 in 𝒫\mathcal{P} (see remark 3.6). The regularity of Γϱ\Gamma_{\varrho} follows from the regularity of uϱu_{\varrho}. Furthermore, we obtain (5.27) by differentiating the relation r⁡(uϱ​(v),v)=ϱr(u_{\varrho}(v),v)=\varrho.

Property PΓ​3\Gamma 3 is showed in [CGNS18, lemma 4.2], whose results hold in the current case as well, since they are proved just by exploiting the signs of κ\kappa and ν\nu (see remark 3.6), the Raychaudhuri equation (2.7), (5.27) and the extension criterion (see theorem 4.1). Lemma 4.2 also shows that the domain of uϱu_{\varrho} is [v1,+∞)[v_{1},+\infty). ∎

Let ϱ∈(r−,r+)\varrho\in(r_{-},r_{+}). Assume that Γϱ≠∅\Gamma_{\varrho}\neq\emptyset and that for every ϵ>0\epsilon>0 there exists v1≥v0v_{1}\geq v_{0} and c>0c>0 such that

If the assumptions of lemma 5.5 are satisfied, the curve Γϱ\Gamma_{\varrho} is spacelike for large values of the vv coordinate. Moreover, v¯<+∞\underline{v}<+\infty and Γϱ∩{v≥v1}⊂𝒯\Gamma_{\varrho}\cap\{v\geq v_{1}\}\subset\mathcal{T}.

5.3 Redshift region

For some fixed RR, chosen close enough to r+r_{+} (see assumption (F)), we now study the region J−​(ΓR)J^{-}(\Gamma_{R}), after proving that it is non-empty.3535 35 By definition (5.25), ΓR={r=R}\Gamma_{R}=\{r=R\} is a (possibly empty) subset of the maximal past set 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Since ν<0\nu<0 in 𝒫\mathcal{P} (see remark 3.6) and due to the extension criterion (theorem 4.1), the curve being empty means that RR is smaller than any value of the area-radius function in [0,U]×[v0,+∞)[0,U]\times[v_{0},+\infty). We will see that this is never the case, i.e. for every choice of v1≥v0v_{1}\geq v_{0} and UU, we can find a curve in [0,U]×[v1,+∞)[0,U]\times[v_{1},+\infty) such that r=Rr=R along it. We denote this set as the redshift region, even though we stress that its location in 𝒫\mathcal{P} is defined through a curve of constant area-radius, rather than of constant shift. Most of the estimates showed in proposition 5.2 propagate throughout the redshift region, and the interplay between the decay of the scalar field and the redshift effect that we observed along the event horizon ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+} (see remark 5.3) is still present, up to an error δ\delta given by the distance of the area-radius rr from r+r_{+}.

To obtain quantitative bounds in this region, it is sufficient to bootstrap the estimates on |ϕ||\phi|, |∂vϕ||\partial_{v}\phi|, |Du​ϕ||D_{u}\phi| and κ\kappa from ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+}, and exploit these to achieve the remaining bounds. In particular, we employ the results of proposition 5.2 and use the smallness of r+−rr_{+}-r to close the bootstrap inequalities.

Proof.

In the following, CℋC_{\mathcal{H}} denotes the constant appearing in the statement of proposition 5.2. We use the letter CC to represent any positive constant depending on the initial data and possibly on η\eta. CK+\displaystyle C_{K_{+}} ≔3​(1+|Λ|3+4r+2​|ϖ+|+24r+4​Q+2),\displaystyle\coloneqq 3\left(1+\frac{|\Lambda|}{3}+\frac{4}{r_{+}^{2}}|\varpi_{+}|+\frac{24}{r_{+}^{4}}Q_{+}^{2}\right), (5.40)

and choose
