The relevant information here is not given by the explicit expressions for the above constants, but rather by the fact that we require the smallness of δ\delta to be dependent only on the initial data and on η\eta.3636 36 Notice that η\eta can ultimately be chosen in terms of the initial data as well. We do not attempt to obtain optimal constants, since such a task would distract from the core idea of the proof.

Setting up the bootstrap procedure: we recall that 𝒫\mathcal{P} is the maximal past set where we can define a solution to the characteristic IVP of section 2.1, with initial data prescribed on [0,U]×{v0}∪{0}×[v0,+∞)[0,U]\times\{v_{0}\}\cup\{0\}\times[v_{0},+\infty). In the following, we consider v1≥v0v_{1}\geq v_{0} to be sufficiently large with respect to the initial data and to η\eta, and define the set

𝒫~≔𝒫∩{(u,v)∈[0,U]×[v1,+∞): 0<r+−r(u,v)≤δ}.\tilde{\mathcal{P}}\coloneqq\mathcal{P}\cap\{(u,v)\in[0,U]\times[v_{1},+\infty)\colon\,0<r_{+}-r(u,v)\leq\delta\}. (5.46)

The latter is non-empty, since the area-radius function provides an increasing parametrization on ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+}, and r⁡(0,v)→r+r(0,v)\to r_{+} as v→+∞v\to+\infty (see (2.50) and (2.54)). Furthermore, 𝒫~\tilde{\mathcal{P}} is connected since it is path-connected: for every couple of points (uA,vA)(u_{A},v_{A}) and (uB,vB)(u_{B},v_{B}) in 𝒫~\tilde{\mathcal{P}}, these can be connected by the path defined as the union of three null segments: the one joining (uA,vA)(u_{A},v_{A}) to (0,vA)(0,v_{A}), the one joining (0,vA)(0,v_{A}) to (0,vB)(0,v_{B}) and, finally, the one joining (0,vB)(0,v_{B}) to (vA,vB)(v_{A},v_{B}). This path is contained in 𝒫~\tilde{\mathcal{P}} by construction.

We now define E\bm{E} as the set of points qq in 𝒫~\tilde{\mathcal{P}} such that the following three inequalities hold for every (u,v)(u,v) in J−​(q)∩𝒫~J^{-}(q)\cap\tilde{\mathcal{P}}:

|ϕ|​(u,v)+|∂vϕ|​(u,v)\displaystyle|\phi|(u,v)+|\partial_{v}\phi|(u,v) ≤4​Cℋ​e−c⁡(s)​v,\displaystyle\leq 4C_{\mathcal{H}}e^{-c(s)v}, (5.47)
|Du​ϕ|​(u,v)\displaystyle|D_{u}\phi|(u,v) ≤M​Cℋ​|ν|​(u,v)​e−c⁡(s)​v,\displaystyle\leq MC_{\mathcal{H}}|\nu|(u,v)e^{-c(s)v}, (5.48)
κ⁡(u,v)\displaystyle\kappa(u,v) ≥12.\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{2}. (5.49)

When s<2​K+−ηs<2K_{+}-\eta, it is immediate to verify that EE contains the subset of the event horizon {(0,v):v≥v1}\{(0,v)\colon\,v\geq v_{1}\}, for any choice of v1≥v0v_{1}\geq v_{0}, due to (5.9), (5.10), (2.45), and to the fact that we chose M>1M>1. On the other hand, for a possibly larger value of v1v_{1}, we also have {(0,v):v≥v1}⊂E\{(0,v)\colon\,v\geq v_{1}\}\subset E for s≥2​K+−ηs\geq 2K_{+}-\eta: indeed, it is sufficient to compare (5.9) with (5.48) and use definition (5.28) to verify that

max⁡{1,v−v0}≤|ν|(0,v)​e−(2​K+−η)​v,\max\{1,v-v_{0}\}\leq|\nu|(0,v)e^{-(2K_{+}-\eta)v}, (5.50)

for vv large. This can be proved as follows. Due to the bound (5.4) for |ν|​(0,⋅)|\nu|(0,\cdot), we have

max⁡{1,v−v0}≤1Cℋ​eη​v≤|ν|​(0,v)​e−(2​K+−η)​v,∀v≥v1,\max\{1,v-v_{0}\}\leq\frac{1}{C_{\mathcal{H}}}e^{\eta v}\leq|\nu|(0,v)e^{-\left(2K_{+}-\eta\right)v},\quad\forall\,v\geq v_{1},

where v1v_{1} is taken sufficiently large with respect to the initial data and to η\eta. This shows the validity of (5.50).

We notice that, since EE is a past set by construction, inequalities (5.47)–(5.49) can be integrated along causal curves ending in (u,v)(u,v) and starting from the event horizon or from the null segment [0,U]×{v1}[0,U]\times\{v_{1}\}.

Outline of the proof: in the following, we show that estimates (5.29)–(5.39) are valid in EE and, at the same time, use this result to close the bootstrap and show that E=𝒫~E=\tilde{\mathcal{P}}. The conclusion then follows after proving that ∅≠J−(ΓR)∩{v≥v1}⊂𝒫~\varnothing\neq J^{-}(\Gamma_{R})\cap\{v\geq v_{1}\}\subset\tilde{\mathcal{P}}.

Closing the bootstrap: let us now fix (u,v)∈E(u,v)\in E. We will prove that, when evaluated at such a point, the quantities |ϕ||\phi|, |∂vϕ||\partial_{v}\phi|, |Du​ϕ||D_{u}\phi| and κ\kappa obey stronger bounds than those in (5.47)–(5.49), i.e. we will show that EE is not only closed in 𝒫~\tilde{\mathcal{P}}, but also an open set. In particular, we will bound the quantities rr, QQ, λ\lambda, ϖ\varpi, KK, κ\kappa, ν\nu, uu, ∂vlog⁡Ω2\partial_{v}\log\Omega^{2}, ϕ\phi, ∂vϕ\partial_{v}\phi and Du​ϕD_{u}\phi in this order.

First, we stress that we have the following bounds on the area-radius function:

{0<r⁡(0,v)−r⁡(u,v)≤r+−r⁡(u,v)≤δ,r⁡(u,v)>r+2,r⁡(u,v)<r+,\begin{cases}0<r(0,v)-r(u,v)\leq r_{+}-r(u,v)\leq\delta,\\ r(u,v)>\frac{r_{+}}{2},\\ r(u,v)<r_{+},\end{cases} (5.51)

due to (5.45), (5.46) and assumption (G).

Now, we use (2.11) and bootstrap inequalities (5.47) and (5.48) to get

|∂uQ|​(u,v)≤4​|q|​M​Cℋ2​r2​(u,v)​|ν|​(u,v)​e−2​c​(s)​v.|\partial_{u}Q|(u,v)\leq 4|q|MC^{2}_{\mathcal{H}}r^{2}(u,v)|\nu|(u,v)e^{-2c(s)v}.

By corollary 5.6 and by (5.62), there exists a C1C^{1} function u↦vR​(u)u\mapsto v_{R}(u) defined for 0≤u≤uR​(v1)0\leq u\leq u_{R}(v_{1}) such that (see also lemma 5.4):

ΓR∩{v≥v1}={(uR(v),v):v≥v1}={(u,vR(u)): 0≤u≤uR(v1)}.\Gamma_{R}\cap\{v\geq v_{1}\}=\{(u_{R}(v),v)\colon\,v\geq v_{1}\}=\{(u,v_{R}(u))\colon\,0\leq u\leq u_{R}(v_{1})\}.

We considered the case v≥v1v\geq v_{1} because (5.62) holds for large values of the vv coordinate. However, notice that we might have

ΓR∩{v≥v1}⊊ΓR,\Gamma_{R}\cap\{v\geq v_{1}\}\subsetneq\Gamma_{R},

see definition (5.25). Since we are going to study solutions to the characteristic IVP restricted to large values of the vv coordinate, we will make no distinction between Γϱ\Gamma_{\varrho} and Γϱ∩{v≥v1}\Gamma_{\varrho}\cap\{v\geq v_{1}\}, for ϱ∈(0,r+)\varrho\in(0,r_{+}), whenever the restriction to large values of vv is clear from the context.

Furthermore, by differentiating the relation r​(u,vR​(u))=Rr(u,v_{R}(u))=R, we can see that

vR′​(u)=−ν​(u,vR​(u))λ​(u,vR​(u))<0.v_{R}^{\prime}(u)=-\frac{\nu(u,v_{R}(u))}{\lambda(u,v_{R}(u))}<0. (5.69)

5.4 Apparent horizon

Assume that the constants η\eta, RR and δ\delta of proposition 5.7 are fixed. This allows us to give a parametrization of the apparent horizon

𝒜={(u,v)∈[0,U]×[v0,+∞):λ(u,v)=0}\mathcal{A}=\{(u,v)\in[0,U]\times[v_{0},+\infty)\colon\,\lambda(u,v)=0\}

and demonstrate that, for large values of the vv coordinate, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a C1C^{1} curve that lies in the causal past of ΓR\Gamma_{R}. We first report a lemma [CGNS18, lemma 3.1], useful to localize the trapped region in the black hole interior. Then, we analyse the set 𝒜∩ΓR\mathcal{A}\cap\Gamma_{R} in the quotient manifold: such a set can only contain isolated points or outgoing null segments of finite length. In the far future, we can be more precise: ΓR\Gamma_{R} never intersects the apparent horizon for large values of vv.

Lemma 5.9 (on the sign of λ\lambda along the outgoing null direction)

Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be the maximal past set where a solution to our characteristic IVP is defined. Take (u,v)∈𝒫(u,v)\in\mathcal{P}. If λ⁡(u,v)=0\lambda(u,v)=0 (respectively, λ⁡(u,v)<0\lambda(u,v)<0), then λ⁡(u,v+V)≤0\lambda(u,v+V)\leq 0 (respectively, λ⁡(u,v+V)<0\lambda(u,v+V)<0) for every V>0V>0 for which (u,v+V)∈𝒫(u,v+V)\in\mathcal{P}.

Proof.

By (2.7):

∂v(λΩ2)≤0.\partial_{v}\left(\frac{\lambda}{\Omega^{2}}\right)\leq 0.

Moreover, by (2.19), (3.4) and (3.8), we know that Ω2=−4​ν​κ>0\Omega^{2}=-4\nu\kappa>0 in 𝒫\mathcal{P}. So, let us assume that λ⁡(u,v)=0\lambda(u,v)=0 (the other case follows similarly). Then, for every V>0V>0 such that (u,v+V)∈𝒫(u,v+V)\in\mathcal{P}:

λΩ2​(u,v)=0 impliesλΩ2​(u,v+V)≤0,\frac{\lambda}{\Omega^{2}}(u,v)=0\quad\text{ implies}\quad\frac{\lambda}{\Omega^{2}}(u,v+V)\leq 0,

and thus λ⁡(u,v+V)≤0\lambda(u,v+V)\leq 0. ∎

Remark 5.10

5.5 No-shift region

In regions corresponding to smaller values of the area-radius, the redshift effect is counterbalanced by a blueshift effect which is expected to originate in the Cauchy horizon (whose existence and stability will be proved as a consequence of the results of section 5). A by-product of this phenomenon is the propagation, throughout this new region, of most of the estimates already obtained in proposition 5.7. We recall that the constants η\eta, δ\delta and RR can be fixed according to the statement of proposition 5.7, and that r−∈(0,r+)r_{-}\in(0,r_{+}) is one of the roots of the function (1−μ)​(⋅,ϖ+,Q+)(1-\mu)(\cdot,\varpi_{+},Q_{+}). A more precise formulation of the above heuristics is then the following: let us choose3737 37 The letter YY, which denotes the constant radius in the region where redshift and blueshift effects balance each other, stands for the yellow color, which lies between the red and blue colors in the visible electromagnetic spectrum. Y∈(r−,R)Y\in(r_{-},R), close enough to r−r_{-}, and work in the set

J+​(ΓR)∩J−​(ΓY),J^{+}(\Gamma_{R})\cap J^{-}(\Gamma_{Y}), (5.72)

which we denote by the name no-shift region, after proving that it is non-empty. The following properties hold in this set:

  • •

    the functions r+−r⁡(⋅,⋅)r_{+}-r(\cdot,\cdot) and r⁡(⋅,⋅)−r−r(\cdot,\cdot)-r_{-} are bounded, but not necessarily δ\delta–small,

  • •

    the surface gravity KK of the dynamical black hole changes sign: it remains positive near ΓR\Gamma_{R} and becomes negative near ΓY\Gamma_{Y}. In this context, we introduce the quantity

    K−≔12​|∂r(1−μ)​(r−,ϖ+,Q+)|,K_{-}\coloneqq\frac{1}{2}\lvert\partial_{r}(1-\mu)(r_{-},\varpi_{+},Q_{+})\rvert, (5.73)

    namely the absolute value of the surface gravity along the Cauchy horizon3838 38 We adopt the convention of [CGNS18, LO19], where K−K_{-} is a positive quantity. In [Moo18], this quantity is defined with the opposite sign. of the final sub-extremal black hole.

In particular, the proof of proposition 5.7, in which the smallness of r+−rr_{+}-r is used to close the bootstrap inequalities, cannot be directly applied to this region. Nonetheless, we can subdivide region (5.72) in finitely many narrow subsets on which we have a finer control on the area-radius function (this technique was also used in [Moo18]). The validity of the respective estimates is then proved in each subset by induction, where the basis step follows from the estimates on the redshift region, while the inductive step is proved with the aid of bootstrap. The bootstrap procedure, in particular, is closed using the smallness of the subsets that partition the no-shift region. A key role will be played by the bound on the geometric quantity 1−μ1-\mu, which lets us relate the quantity ν\nu defined in this region to ν|ΓR\nu_{|\Gamma_{R}}. We stress that, in the uncharged case [CGNS18], the bound on 1−μ1-\mu could be obtained directly from the monotonicity of the renormalized Hawking mass. Such a property is not present in the current case.

Differently from the redshift region, the estimates in the no-shift region involve constants depending not only on the initial data and on η\eta, but also on RR and YY (mainly due to the bound on 1−μ1-\mu). This requires additional care in the bootstrap methods adopted in the next regions, since we want the final result to be independent of the partition of the black hole interior. Ultimately, we will fix such constants in terms of the initial data only (see for instance the forthcoming proposition 5.13 for the constraint on YY).

5.6 Early blueshift region: general behaviour

In the next steps, we inspect the consequences of the blueshift effect in the region J+​(ΓY)J^{+}(\Gamma_{Y}). Here and in the following, the constants η\eta, δ\delta, RR can be fixed according to the statement of proposition 5.7. The value of v1v_{1} given by the same proposition, will possibly increase. The constants Δ\Delta and YY of proposition 5.12 will be prescribed in the next steps in terms of bounds that depend only on the initial data. Then, given a real number β\beta such that4141 41 The upper bound for β\beta was chosen so that some exponential terms controlling the main PDE variables decay, see also the proof of proposition 5.13 and of lemma 5.17.

0<β<c⁡(s)7​K−,0<\beta<\frac{c(s)}{7K_{-}}, (5.117)

with c⁡(s)c(s) given in (5.28), we define the curve

γ≔{(u,(1+β)​vY​(u)):u∈[0,uY​(v1)]}.\gamma\coloneqq\{(u,(1+\beta)v_{Y}(u))\colon\,u\in[0,u_{Y}(v_{1})]\}. (5.118)

For a suitably large choice of v1v_{1}, the curve γ\gamma is spacelike, since that is the case for ΓY={(u,vY​(u)):u∈[0,uY​(v1)]}\Gamma_{Y}=\{(u,v_{Y}(u))\colon u\in[0,u_{Y}(v_{1})]\}. Indeed, after recalling the expression of gg in (2.3), it is immediate to verify that g⁡(X,X)>0g(X,X)>0, X=∂u+(1+β)vY′∂vX=\partial_{u}+(1+\beta)v^{\prime}_{Y}\partial_{v} being the vector field tangent to γ\gamma. We also use the notation

vγ​(u)≔(1+β)​vY​(u),∀u∈[0,uY​(v1)],v_{\gamma}(u)\coloneqq(1+\beta)v_{Y}(u),\quad\forall\,u\in[0,u_{Y}(v_{1})],

and uγu_{\gamma} denotes the map that gives a parametrization of the curve as γ={(uγ(v),v):v∈[v1,+∞)}\gamma=\{(u_{\gamma}(v),v)\colon\,v\in[v_{1},+\infty)\}, similarly to the functions uRu_{R} and uYu_{Y} used so far.

The aim of the curve γ\gamma is to probe a spacetime region where the blueshift effect starts to be relevant, but whose influence is weak enough so that the quantities describing the dynamical black hole can be controlled as done in the previously inspected regions. This is why we denote the region

J+​(ΓY)∩J−​(γ)J^{+}(\Gamma_{Y})\cap J^{-}(\gamma)

by the name early blueshift region.

Here the dynamical solution is still quantitatively close to the final sub-extremal Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter black hole, in the sense that ϖ\varpi converges to ϖ+\varpi_{+} and QQ converges to Q+Q_{+} at an exponential rate. However, due to the non-zero value of β\beta (which distinguishes γ\gamma from a curve of constant radius), we lose decay with respect to the no-shift region. Also, although this region is delimited by a curve of constant area-radius only in the past, the function rr is still bounded away from zero for v1v_{1} large.

Some technical difficulties, which were absent in the uncharged Λ>0\Lambda>0 case and in the charged Λ=0\Lambda=0 case, arise in this region. Differently from [CGNS15a] and [CGNS18], we cannot directly apply BV estimates (originally presented in [Daf05a]) on the quantities Du​ϕD_{u}\phi and ∂vϕ\partial_{v}\phi, due to new terms in equations (2.27) and (2.28) that were absent in the uncharged case. We then prove the results by bootstrap, similarly to the procedure followed in the redshift region, where now we close the bootstrap inequalities by exploiting the smallness of r−r−r-r_{-}. The procedure differs from the bootstrap technique used in [Moo18], since in our case we cannot take N​ϵN\epsilon large (where NN and ϵ=ϵ⁡(N)\epsilon=\epsilon(N) are defined in the no-shift region) to improve our inequalities. Indeed, since the no-shift region in the current case is enclosed between two curves of constant area-radius, we have that N​ϵ=R−YN\epsilon=R-Y.

A prominent role in the proof is played by 𝒞s\mathcal{C}_{s}, a function in both the uu and vv coordinates that we define and that determines the exponential decay of the main quantities. This function replaces the linear function v↦c⁡(s)​vv\mapsto c(s)v of the previous regions. The aim of 𝒞s\mathcal{C}_{s} is to interpolate between the exponential decay known along the curve ΓY\Gamma_{Y} (see proposition 5.12) and the one expected along γ\gamma (see [CGNS18]), so that the function |ν|​exp⁡(−𝒞s)|\nu|\exp(-\mathcal{C}_{s}), appearing in many integral estimates, is monotonically increasing in vv. In particular, 𝒞s\mathcal{C}_{s} is chosen in such a way that it is monotonic in both coordinates, so that the main integral estimates of this region can be achieved similarly to the ones of the redshift and no-shift regions.

Proposition 5.13 (estimates in the early blueshift region)

Let β\beta be a constant satisfying (5.117), and let η\eta, δ\delta and RR be the constants given by proposition 5.7. Then, for every ε>0\varepsilon>0 small enough, depending only on the initial data, there exists Δ∈(0,ε)\Delta\in(0,\varepsilon), Y>0Y>0 such that

0<Y−r−<Δ,0<Y-r_{-}<\Delta, (5.119)

and v1=v1​(ε,η,R,Y)≥v0v_{1}=v_{1}(\varepsilon,\eta,R,Y)\geq v_{0}, defining the curve γ\gamma as in (5.118) and such that the following inequalities hold for every (u,v)∈J+(ΓY)∩J−(γ)∩{v≥v1}(u,v)\in J^{+}(\Gamma_{Y})\cap J^{-}(\gamma)\cap\{v\geq v_{1}\}:

r⁡(u,v)\displaystyle r(u,v) ≥r−−ε,\displaystyle\geq r_{-}-\varepsilon, (5.120)

|Q⁡(u,v)−Q+|\displaystyle|Q(u,v)-Q_{+}| ≤C​e−2​𝒞s​(u,v),\displaystyle\leq Ce^{-2\mathcal{C}_{s}(u,v)}, (5.122)
|K⁡(u,v)+K−|\displaystyle|K(u,v)+K_{-}| ≤C​ε,\displaystyle\leq C\varepsilon, (5.123)

where C>0C>0 depends on the initial data and possibly on η\eta, RR and YY; K−K_{-} is given by (5.73); we defined

for some C~>0\tilde{C}>0 depending uniquely on the initial data, and c⁡(s)c(s) was defined in (5.28).

We observe that:

    for (u,v)∈J+​(ΓY)∩J−​(γ)(u,v)\in J^{+}(\Gamma_{Y})\cap J^{-}(\gamma), vv large and for any α>1\alpha>1.

Remark 5.18 (on the estimates along the curve γ\gamma)

As β\beta tends to zero (see (5.117)), the curve γ\gamma approaches the curve of constant radius ΓY\Gamma_{Y}. The importance of a non-zero value for β\beta is apparent in the results of lemma 5.17, showing that, along γ\gamma:

  • •

    Not only the quantity |λ||\lambda| is bounded (as occurs in the redshift, no-shift and early blueshift regions, see (5.30), (5.74) and (5.142)) but it also decays at a rate which is integrable in [v1,+∞)[v_{1},+\infty); this result will be vital to prove that rr is bounded and bounded away from zero at the Cauchy horizon;

  • •

We also notice that, in J+​(ΓY)∩J−​(γ)J^{+}(\Gamma_{Y})\cap J^{-}(\gamma), requiring UU to be small is equivalent to requiring suitably large values of v1v_{1}, due to the spacelike nature of γ\gamma and its location in the black hole interior. and a similar relation holds for points along γ\gamma, since vY​(u)=(1+β)−1​vγ​(u)v_{Y}(u)=(1+\beta)^{-1}v_{\gamma}(u). On the other hand, in the region J+​(γ)J^{+}(\gamma) the restrictions on the vv coordinate do not constrain the ingoing null coordinate.

5.8 Late blueshift region

In the causal future of the curve γ\gamma, also dubbed the late blueshift region, the dynamical black hole departs considerably4343 43 By this, we mean that we have less control on the main dynamical quantities, e.g. KK and ϖ\varpi, with respect to the previous regions that we analysed. A precise notion of ‘distance’ between the dynamical black-hole and the fixed sub-extremal Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter solution depends on the norm used to control the PDE variables. from the fixed sub-extremal solution. After showing that estimates (5.157) and (5.158) propagate to J+​(γ)J^{+}(\gamma), it will follow that rr remains bounded away from zero in this entire region. This will be the key ingredient to show the existence, for the dynamical model, of a Cauchy horizon 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+} beyond which the metric gg can be continuously extended. We stress that our construction of γ\gamma, positioned sufficiently close to ΓY\Gamma_{Y}, is what allows us to propagate decaying estimates throughout J+​(γ)J^{+}(\gamma) despite the adverse contribution of the blueshift effect.

The core idea of the proof is again a bootstrap argument involving the quantity ∂vϕ\partial_{v}\phi. The proof, however, differs significantly from the bootstrap procedures of the previous regions, due to the lack of an upper bound4444 44 The main obstructions to this result stemming from the quadratic term |Du​ϕ|2|D_{u}\phi|^{2} in (2.38) and the term κ−1\kappa^{-1} in (2.26). The renormalized Hawking mass was shown to blow up in the real and massless case [CGNS18] for a class of initial data and by further assuming a lower bound on |∂vϕ||\partial_{v}\phi| along the event horizon. on the quantities |ϖ||\varpi| and |K||K| and due to the absence of a lower bound on κ\kappa. A natural way to close the argument is to control ϕ\phi and Du​ϕD_{u}\phi by integrating the estimate on ∂vϕ\partial_{v}\phi that we bootstrap from γ\gamma. This is also possible due to a bound on ∂vlog⁡Ω2\partial_{v}\log\Omega^{2}, which is related to KK via (2.41).

The technical difficulties of the proof can be summarised as follows. Due to the presence of the non-constant charge function QQ, we cannot apply the soft analysis used in [CGNS15a, CGNS18] to propagate the bounds on |ν||\nu| and |λ||\lambda| from the curve γ\gamma. A bootstrap argument lets us circumvent this difficulty and obtain additional estimates on |ϕ||\phi|, |∂vϕ||\partial_{v}\phi|, |Du​ϕ||D_{u}\phi| and |Q||Q|. A core ingredient of the proof is given by a bound on ∂vlog⁡Ω2\partial_{v}\log\Omega^{2}, quantity which plays a crucial role in [Moo18].

Lemma 5.20

For every ε~>0\tilde{\varepsilon}>0 small, there exists Uε~>0U_{\tilde{\varepsilon}}>0 such that

r⁡(u,v)>r−−2​ε~r(u,v)>r_{-}-2\tilde{\varepsilon}

for every (u,v)(u,v) in J+(γ)∩{u<Uε~}J^{+}(\gamma)\cap\{u<U_{\tilde{\varepsilon}}\}.

Proof.

The proof is analogous to the one of lemma 7.2 in [CGNS15a], where the results on ν\nu and λ\lambda exploited in such a proof can be replaced with those of proposition 5.19. ∎

Corollary 5.21

Let Uε~>0U_{\tilde{\varepsilon}}>0 be the value provided by lemma 5.20 for some ε~<r−2\tilde{\varepsilon}<\frac{r_{-}}{2}. Then:

[0,Uε~]×[v0,+∞)⊂𝒫,[0,U_{\tilde{\varepsilon}}]\times[v_{0},+\infty)\subset\mathcal{P},

and the estimates of proposition 5.19 hold in J+(γ)∩{u<Uε~}J^{+}(\gamma)\cap\{u<U_{\tilde{\varepsilon}}\}. Moreover, the limit

limv→+∞r⁡(u,v)\lim_{v\to+\infty}r(u,v)

exists and is finite for every u∈[0,Uε~]u\in[0,U_{\tilde{\varepsilon}}], and

limu→0limv→+∞r⁡(u,v)=r−.\lim_{u\to 0}\lim_{v\to+\infty}r(u,v)=r_{-}.
Proof.

The inclusion follows from the extension criterion (theorem 4.1) and lemma 5.20. The limits are well-defined by the monotonicity of rr in J+​(γ)J^{+}(\gamma), namely the fact that λ<0\lambda<0 (see (5.74) and lemma 5.9) and ν<0\nu<0. The final limit follows from lemma 5.20. ∎

5.9 A continuous extension

The construction obtained so far allows us to represent the Cauchy horizon 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+} of the dynamical black hole as the level set of a regular function. In particular, let (u,V)(u,V) be a new coordinate system defined as follows. Given a sufficiently regular function f:[v0,+∞)→ℝf\colon[v_{0},+\infty)\to\mathbb{R} such that the limit of its first derivative as v→+∞v\to+\infty exists and

d​f​(v)d​v​⟶v→+∞−2​K−,\frac{df(v)}{dv}\underset{v\to+\infty}{\longrightarrow}-2K_{-}, (5.198)

we define

V(v)≔1−∫v+∞ef⁡(y)dy,∀v∈[v0,+∞).V(v)\coloneqq 1-\int_{v}^{+\infty}e^{f(y)}dy,\quad\forall\,v\in[v_{0},+\infty). (5.199)

We stress that (5.198) implies that the above integral is finite for every v∈[v0,+∞)v\in[v_{0},+\infty). The choice f⁡(v)=−2​K−​vf(v)=-2K_{-}v was taken into account in [LO19] to construct a continuous extension in the case Λ=0\Lambda=0, where the authors studied the evolution of two-ended asymptotically flat initial data. Here, we are going to consider any function ff such that

d​f​(v)d​v=2K(uγ(v),v),∀v∈[v0,+∞),\frac{df(v)}{dv}=2K(u_{\gamma}(v),v),\quad\forall\,v\in[v_{0},+\infty), (5.200)

as done in [KM22]. This gives, specifically,

𝒞​ℋ+=V−1​({1}).\mathcal{CH}^{+}=V^{-1}(\{1\}).

The solutions to our IVP expressed in the coordinate system (u,V)(u,V) will be denoted by a subscript, e.g. rV​(u,V)=r⁡(u,v)r_{V}(u,V)=r(u,v) and λV​(u,V)=∂VrV​(u,V)=e−f⁡(v)​λ​(u,v)\lambda_{V}(u,V)=\partial_{V}r_{V}(u,V)=e^{-f(v)}\lambda(u,v). We designate the smallest value that VV can take by V0=V⁡(v0)V_{0}=V(v_{0}).

In the following, we restrict the range of the ingoing null coordinate to the set [0,U][0,U], where we use again the letter UU to denote a value chosen sufficiently small, so that corollary 5.21 holds for some fixed ε~<r−2\tilde{\varepsilon}<\frac{r_{-}}{2}. This also implies that J+(γ)∩{u≤U}=J+(γ)J^{+}(\gamma)\cap\{u\leq U\}=J^{+}(\gamma).

In this context, we show that the metric gg and the scalar field ϕ\phi admit a continuous extension beyond the Cauchy horizon, in the sense of theorem 11.1 in [Daf05a]. This is a strong signal for the potential failure of conjecture 1.1, whose definitive resolution however requires a complementary study of the exterior problem.

6 No-mass-inflation scenario and H1H^{1} extensions

Heuristics and numerical work (see section 1.4) suggest the validity of the exponential Price law upper bound (2.49) along the event horizon of a solution asymptotically approaching (in the sense of section 2.2) a Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter black hole. Compared to the case Λ=0\Lambda=0, however, the exact asymptotics given by the constant value ss in (2.49) play an even more important role, since the redshift (resp. blueshift) effect is expected to give an exponential contribution to the decay (resp. growth) of the main dynamical quantities: the value of ss then determines the leading exponential contribution. This has a decisive role in determining the final fate of the dynamical black hole: a dominance of the blueshift effect is expected to cause geometric quantities such as the renormalized Hawking mass to blow up at the Cauchy horizon (mass inflation), whereas a sufficient fast decay of the scalar field along ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+} may allow to extend the dynamical quantities across the Cauchy horizon in such a way that they are still weak solutions to the Einstein-Maxwell-charged-Klein-Gordon system (lack of global uniqueness).

In [CGNS18], where the massless, real scalar field model was studied, any positive value of ss was allowed and a further lower bound on the scalar field was assumed along the event horizon.5050 50 With respect to our exponential Price law, the work [CGNS18] uses a different convention. For every ϵ>0\epsilon>0, they choose initial data such that e−(S​K++ϵ)​v≲|∂vϕ|(0,v)≲e−(S​K+−ϵ)​ve^{-(SK_{+}+\epsilon)v}\lesssim|\partial_{v}\phi|(0,v)\lesssim e^{-(SK_{+}-\epsilon)v} along the event horizon, for some S>0S>0. There, different relations between ss and the quantity5151 51 See also appendix A in [CGNS17] for a proof of the positivity of ρ−1\rho-1. The case ρ=1\rho=1 is associated to extremal black holes.

ρ≔K−K+>1\rho\coloneqq\frac{K_{-}}{K_{+}}>1 (6.1)

led to different outcomes. They found a set in the ρ−s\rho-s plane for which mass inflation can be excluded for generic initial data: in this context, an H1H^{1} extension of the solution was built and the so-called Christodoulou-Chruściel version of strong cosmic censorship was called into question. On the other hand, they found another set in the ρ−s\rho-s plane, disjoint from the previous one, for which mass inflation was guaranteed. This suggests that the H1H^{1} version of the strong cosmic censorship, in this spherically symmetric toy model with Λ>0\Lambda>0, does hold if such initial data can be attained when starting the evolution from a suitable spacelike hypersurface.

In the following, by requiring an upper bound (but no lower bound) on the scalar field along the event horizon (see (2.49)) we prove, despite the lack of many monotonicity results, that mass inflation can be avoided generically5252 52 Provided that ρ\rho and ss satisfy (6.2). We emphasize that, to study the admissibility of such values of ρ\rho and ss, a rigorous analysis of the exterior problem is required. Although it has been established [Dya15, BZ97] that the value of ss corresponding to the decay of the (real or complex) scalar field along ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+} is determined by the spectral gap of the Laplace-Beltrami operator, a rigorous determination of such ss is still generally lacking. also in the massive and charged case. With respect to the case of the real scalar field, we extend the set of possible values of ss for which H1H^{1} extensions can be constructed (see Fig. 2), in agreement with the results obtained for the linear problem [CF17, HV17].

Also in this section, we set UU as the maximum of the ingoing null coordinate, where UU is chosen suitably small, so that corollary 5.21 holds for a fixed ε~<r−2\tilde{\varepsilon}<\frac{r_{-}}{2}.

6.1 No mass inflation

Theorem 6.1 (A sufficient condition to prevent mass inflation)

Given the characteristic IVP of section 2.1, choose initial data for which

s>K− and ρ=K−K+<2s>K_{-}\quad\text{ and }\quad\rho=\frac{K_{-}}{K_{+}}<2 (6.2)

|ϖ|​(u,v)≤C,∀(u,v)∈J+​(γ),|\varpi|(u,v)\leq C,\quad\forall\,(u,v)\in J^{+}(\gamma),

provided that the value of UU is sufficiently small.

Remark 6.2

The linear analysis performed in [CF17] shows the analogue of a no-mass-inflation regime in the entire region K−<min⁡{s,2​K+}K_{-}<\min\{s,2K_{+}\}. This coincides with the region of the ρ−s\rho-s plane given in theorem 6.1 (see also Fig. 2). The linear analysis in [HV17] presents, using different techniques, an analogous result where the regularity of the extension depends on the decay of the initial data.

Remark 6.3 (On mass inflation)

In [CGNS18], sufficient conditions to show the presence of mass inflation were found. By assuming a lower bound on the scalar field along the event horizon, namely by requiring

e−(S​K++ε)​v≲|∂vϕ|(0,v)≲e−(S​K+−ε)​v,e^{-(SK_{+}+\varepsilon)v}\lesssim|\partial_{v}\phi|(0,v)\lesssim e^{-(SK_{+}-\varepsilon)v},

for 0<S<min⁡{ρ,2}0<S<\min\{\rho,2\} and ε>0\varepsilon>0, it was possible to show that limv→+∞|ϖ|(u,v)=+∞\lim_{v\to+\infty}|\varpi|(u,v)=+\infty, for every u∈]0,U]u\in]0,U].

In the charged scalar field case, oscillations affect this scenario and integral bounds for |∂vϕ||\partial_{v}\phi| are expected to be more relevant. Furthermore, the monotonicity of the quantities ϖ\varpi, θ\theta, ζ\zeta and κ\kappa play a prominent role in the proof of the above result in the real, massless case. In particular, in [CGNS18], it was possible to prove that the mass inflation scenario is strongly related with the behaviour of the integral in (6.4). In particular, in the real and massless case:

  1. 1.

    The convergence of the integral in (6.4) implies

    ∫vγ​(u)v|θ|2|λ|​(u,v′)​d​v′→0, as ​u→0,\int_{v_{\gamma}(u)}^{v}\frac{|\theta|^{2}}{|\lambda|}(u,v^{\prime})dv^{\prime}\to 0,\quad\text{ as }u\to 0,

    whereas in the current case it is not even clear if the limit is well-defined. Even working with subsequences does not allow to immediately control the quantity ϖ\varpi.

  2. 2.

    The lower bound on the scalar field can be propagated from the event horizon to J+​(γ)J^{+}(\gamma), due to the positivity of ζ\zeta and θ\theta in J+​(𝒜)J^{+}(\mathcal{A}). In the current case, on the other hand, the system does not include such explicit monotonicity properties (for instance we recall that ζ\zeta, θ\theta and ϕ\phi are complex-valued quantities).

6.2 Construction of an H1H^{1} extension

By prescribing initial data such that conditions (6.2) are satisfied, we proved that the solution to the Einstein-Maxwell-charged-Klein-Gordon system admits a non-trivial Cauchy horizon 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+}, along which |ϖ||\varpi| remains bounded. In this context, we now prove that such a solution further admits an Hloc1H^{1}_{\text{loc}} extension up to its Cauchy horizon, namely we show that all PDE variables of the IVP (except possibly for the ones corresponding, in a different coordinate system, to θ\theta and κ\kappa) admit a continuous extension, that the Christoffel symbols can be extended in Lloc2L^{2}_{\text{loc}} and that ϕ\phi can be extended in Hloc1H^{1}_{\text{loc}}.

Extensions in such a class represent the minimal requirement to understand the extended spacetimes as weak solutions to the Einstein equations. We stress that we required enough regularity so that the second-order PDE system under consideration is equivalent to the first-order system (2.20)–(2.33) (see also remark 3.5). It is interesting to notice that, if less regularity is demanded, it is a priori possible to construct metric extensions beyond the Cauchy horizon that solve the first-order system but not the second-order system of PDEs.

In the current case, the fact that our extensions solve the second-order system of PDEs in a weak sense beyond 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+} is a corollary of previous work [GL19], see also remark 6.8.

To construct the Hloc1H^{1}_{\text{loc}} extension, we first introduce the coordinate

v~​(v)≔r⁡(U,v𝒜​(U))−r⁡(U,v),\tilde{v}(v)\coloneqq r(U,v_{\mathcal{A}}(U))-r(U,v),

where v𝒜​(U)≔max⁡{v:λ⁡(U,v)=0}v_{\mathcal{A}}(U)\coloneqq\max\{v\colon\lambda(U,v)=0\} (see also corollary 5.11 for a localization and the main properties of the apparent horizon). We provide a further C0C^{0} extension in the (u,v~)(u,\tilde{v}) coordinate system, which will be used to construct an Hloc1H^{1}_{\text{loc}} extension. We will denote the solutions to our IVP in the coordinate system (u,v~)(u,\tilde{v}) by a tilde, e.g. r~​(u,v~)=r​(u,v)\tilde{r}(u,\tilde{v})=r(u,v) and λ~​(u,v~)=∂v~r~​(u,v~)=−λ⁡(u,v)λ⁡(U,v)\tilde{\lambda}(u,\tilde{v})=\partial_{\tilde{v}}\tilde{r}(u,\tilde{v})=-\frac{\lambda(u,v)}{\lambda(U,v)}. In this coordinate system, the Cauchy horizon can be expressed as a level set: 𝒞​ℋ+=v~−1​(V~)\mathcal{CH}^{+}=\tilde{v}^{-1}(\tilde{V}), for some positive constant V~\tilde{V}. Moreover, we denote v~0≔v~​(v0)\tilde{v}_{0}\coloneqq\tilde{v}(v_{0}).

In order to establish an Hloc1H^{1}_{\text{loc}} extension, we use a further coordinate v̊\mathring{v} defined by the equality

Ω̊2​(U,v̊)≡1,\mathring{\Omega}^{2}(U,\mathring{v})\equiv 1, (6.15)

where the circle superscript is used here and in the following to denote PDE variables expressed in this newly-defined coordinate. Expression (6.15), together with (2.19) and (2.33), entails, in particular, that

d​v̊d​v=Ω2​(U,v).\frac{d\mathring{v}}{dv}=\Omega^{2}(U,v).

Similarly to the previous cases, we denote v̊0≔v̊​(v0)\mathring{v}_{0}\coloneqq\mathring{v}(v_{0}).

The coordinate systems (u,v~)(u,\tilde{v}) and (u,v̊)(u,\mathring{v}) were used in [CGNS18, section 12], where their C1C^{1}-compatibility up to the Cauchy horizon and the finiteness of V̊≔v̊​(V~)\mathring{V}\coloneqq\mathring{v}(\tilde{V}) were shown.5555 55 In particular, every C0C^{0} extension in the (u,v~)(u,\tilde{v}) coordinate system gives rise to a C0C^{0} extension in the (u,v̊)(u,\mathring{v}) coordinate system, and vice versa.

Theorem 6.4

Suppose that the assumptions of theorem 6.1 hold. Then, for every 0<δU<U0<\delta_{U}<U, the functions λ~\tilde{\lambda}, ϖ~\tilde{\varpi}, ϕ~\tilde{\phi}, Q~\tilde{Q}, r~\tilde{r}, ν~\tilde{\nu}, ζ~\tilde{\zeta}, A~u\tilde{A}_{u} (but not necessarily θ~\tilde{\theta} or κ~\tilde{\kappa}) admit a continuous extension to [δU,U]×[0,V~][\delta_{U},U]\times[0,\tilde{V}].

Proof.

q~​(u,V~)≔limv~→V~q~​(u,v~)\tilde{q}(u,\tilde{V})\coloneqq\lim_{\tilde{v}\to\tilde{V}}\tilde{q}(u,\tilde{v})

exists, is finite and that

|q~​(u,v~)−q~​(u,V~)|​⟶v~→V~​0uniformly in ​[δU,U].\left|\tilde{q}(u,\tilde{v})-\tilde{q}(u,\tilde{V})\right|\underset{\tilde{v}\to\tilde{V}}{\longrightarrow}0\quad\text{uniformly in }[\delta_{U},U].

Alternatively, it is sufficient to show that q~\tilde{q} can be expressed in terms of quantities that can be extended.

For the sake of convenience, we define

f⁡(v)≔v~​(v)=r⁡(U,v𝒜​(U))−r⁡(U,v),f(v)\coloneqq\tilde{v}(v)=r(U,v_{\mathcal{A}}(U))-r(U,v), (6.16)

for every v∈[v0,+∞)v\in[v_{0},+\infty). To extend r~\tilde{r}, we first observe that r~​(⋅,V~)\tilde{r}(\cdot,\tilde{V}) is well-defined by monotonicity. Moreover, for every u∈[δU,U]u\in[\delta_{U},U], (5.172) implies

uniformly in [δU,U][\delta_{U},U]. Due to the fundamental theorem of calculus, this entails that r~​(⋅,v~)\tilde{r}(\cdot,\tilde{v}) converges to r~​(⋅,V~)\tilde{r}(\cdot,\tilde{V}) uniformly in [δU,U][\delta_{U},U].

Let us now deal with ϖ~\tilde{\varpi}. By (6.3) and due to the estimates of proposition 5.19, it is clear that we only need to verify the convergence of ∫|θ~|2|λ~|​(u,z)​𝑑z\int\frac{|\tilde{\theta}|^{2}}{|\tilde{\lambda}|}(u,z)dz. uniformly in uu (in fact, |θ​λ−1||\theta\lambda^{-1}| is a geometric quantity and the factor coming from θ~\tilde{\theta} cancels out with the Jacobian of the change of variables). The charge Q~\tilde{Q} can be extended in a similar way: by (2.31) we have

Remark 6.5

The existence of a continuous extension for κ~\tilde{\kappa} in theorem 6.4 relies on the behaviour of ν~\tilde{\nu}: if ν~\tilde{\nu} extends to 0 along the Cauchy horizon 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+}, then κ~\tilde{\kappa} has to diverge at 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+} in such a way that

is a positive and bounded quantity in [δU,U]×{V~}[\delta_{U},U]\times\{\tilde{V}\}. Notice that the extendibility of κ~\tilde{\kappa} is not required in theorem 12.3 in [CGNS18], where an Hloc1H^{1}_{\text{loc}} extension is constructed.

Corollary 6.7

Let M0M_{0} be the preimage of (0,U]×[v̊0,V̊](0,U]\times[\mathring{v}_{0},\mathring{V}] via the coordinate functions (u,v̊)(u,\mathring{v}). Then, the pull-backed scalar field and Christoffel symbols on M0M_{0} are, respectively, in Hloc1​(M0)H^{1}_{\text{loc}}(M_{0}) and Lloc2​(M0)L^{2}_{\text{loc}}(M_{0}).

Proof.

For every 0<δU<U0<\delta_{U}<U, we denote by ℳδ\mathcal{M}_{\delta} the preimage of [δU,U]×[v̊0,V̊][\delta_{U},U]\times[\mathring{v}_{0},\mathring{V}] via the coordinate functions (u,v̊)(u,\mathring{v}). The volume form on ℳδ\mathcal{M}_{\delta} is

d​V4=Ω̊22​r̊2​d​u​d​v̊.dV_{4}=\frac{\mathring{\Omega}^{2}}{2}\mathring{r}^{2}dud\mathring{v}.

Since r̊\mathring{r} and Ω̊2\mathring{\Omega}^{2} are continuous in the compact set [δU,U]×[v̊0,V̊][\delta_{U},U]\times[\mathring{v}_{0},\mathring{V}], the results of theorem 6.6 are sufficient to conclude the proof. ∎

Remark 6.8 (Extensions beyond the Cauchy horizon as weak solutions)

In the asymptotically flat, extremal case studied in [GL19, sec. 10], it was explicitly shown how to construct H1H^{1} extensions solving (in a weak sense) the second-order system of PDEs beyond the Cauchy horizon 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+}.

The procedure exploits a well-posedness result, under spherical symmetry, that requires less regularity for the initial data, compared to our local existence theorem 3.2. The result then follows after considering a sequence of characteristic initial value problems approaching the Cauchy horizon and using the fact that the time of existence for the respective solutions does not depend on the location of such IVP in the sequence.

Due to the freedom in defining the main extendable PDE variables beyond the Cauchy horizon, the technique reveals the existence of infinitely many weak solutions beyond 𝒞​ℋ+\mathcal{CH}^{+}.

We stress that the same procedure can be applied in our case, since the presence of the cosmological constant Λ\Lambda in our second-order system (2.6)–(2.10), (2.30)–(2.31) does not represent an obstruction to the reasoning of [GL19], and neither does the sub-extremality condition.

Appendix B The Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter solution and the choice of coordinates

In this short section we review the main properties of spherically symmetric charged black holes. At the same time, we establish the relation between the null coordinates employed in this work and some Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates commonly adopted for the Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter solution.

The (sub-extremal, or non-degenerate) Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter metric is the unique static, spherically symmetric solution of the electro-vacuum Einstein equations

Ricμ​ν​(g)−12​R​(g)​gμ​ν+Λ​gμ​ν=2​gα​β​Fα​μ​Fβ​ν−12​gμ​ν​Fα​β​Fα​β,\text{Ric}_{\mu\nu}(g)-\frac{1}{2}R(g)g_{\mu\nu}+\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}=2g^{\alpha\beta}F_{\alpha\mu}F_{\beta\nu}-\frac{1}{2}g_{\mu\nu}F^{\alpha\beta}F_{\alpha\beta},

for a positive cosmological constant Λ\Lambda. Here, the strength field tensor FF satisfies the Maxwell equations d​F=0dF=0 and d⋆F=0d\star F=0. This solution is denoted by the three real constants ϖ+>0\varpi_{+}>0 (mass parameter), Q+Q_{+} (charge parameter) and Λ\Lambda.5757 57 This notation for the mass and charge is not standard, but we adopt it here to draw a comparison with our work on the Einstein-Maxwell-charged-Klein-Gordon system. To such values, we associate the function

1−f⁡(r)≔1−2​ϖ+r+Q+2r2−Λ3​r2,1-f(r)\coloneqq 1-\frac{2\varpi_{+}}{r}+\frac{Q_{+}^{2}}{r^{2}}-\frac{\Lambda}{3}r^{2},

required to have three distinct real roots r−r_{-}, r+r_{+} and rCr_{C}, with r−<r+<rCr_{-}<r_{+}<r_{C} (sub-extremality assumption). In general, 1−f1-f may possess a fourth distinct (negative) root, which we denote by rnr_{n}. The Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter metric, able to describe a black hole spacetime in an expanding cosmological scenario, can be written in coordinates (t,r)∈ℝ×(r−,r+)(t,r)\in\mathbb{R}\times(r_{-},r_{+}) as

gRNdS=−(1−f⁡(r))​d​t2+11−f⁡(r)​d​r2+r2​σS2,g_{\text{RNdS}}=-\left(1-f(r)\right)dt^{2}+\frac{1}{1-f(r)}dr^{2}+r^{2}\sigma_{S^{2}}, (B.1)

where σS2\sigma_{S^{2}} is the standard metric on the unit round sphere. We refer the reader to [CF17, CG20] for an overview on this spacetime, on the different coordinate systems to resolve the coordinate singularities at r=r+r=r_{+} (corresponding to the event horizon ℋRNdS+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{\text{RNdS}}) and r=r−r=r_{-} (corresponding to the Cauchy horizon 𝒞​ℋRNdS+\mathcal{CH}^{+}_{\text{RNdS}}), and on the failure of determinism inherent in this non-generic solution.

We now show that the outgoing null coordinate chosen in section 2.2 for our Einstein-Maxwell-charged-Klein-Gordon system is strictly related to the outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein coordinate

v~=r∗+t2,with ​r∗≔∫d​r1−f⁡(r),\tilde{v}=\frac{r^{*}+t}{2},\quad\text{with }r^{*}\coloneqq\int\frac{dr}{1-f(r)}, (B.2)

that can be used to describe regions of the Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter spacetime close to the event horizon ℋRNdS+\mathcal{H}_{\text{RNdS}}^{+}. As we will see, this result implies that the v\bm{v} coordinate in the exponential Price law upper bound (2.49) is half of the outgoing Eddington-Finkelstein coordinate adopted for the linear analyses [CF17] and [HV17]. This is of particular interest in the cosmological scenario, since different coordinate choices could lead to different exponential behaviours of the scalar field along the event horizon ℋ+\mathcal{H}^{+} of the dynamical black hole.

In particular, using the Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates

u~=r∗−t2,v~=r∗+t2,\tilde{u}=\frac{r^{*}-t}{2},\qquad\tilde{v}=\frac{r^{*}+t}{2},

and then the coordinate

u=12​K+​e2​K+​u~,u=\frac{1}{2K_{+}}e^{2K_{+}\tilde{u}},

where K+K_{+} is the surface gravity of ℋRNdS+\mathcal{H}^{+}_{\text{RNdS}}, we can write (B.1) as

gRNdS\displaystyle g_{\text{RNdS}} =4​(1−f⁡(r⁡(u~,v~)))​d​u~​d​v~+r2​(u~,v~)​σS2\displaystyle=4\big(1-f(r(\tilde{u},\tilde{v}))\big)d\tilde{u}d\tilde{v}+r^{2}(\tilde{u},\tilde{v})\sigma_{S^{2}}
=4​e−2​K+​u~​(u)​(1−f⁡(r⁡(u,v~)))​d​u​d​v~+r2​(u,v~)​σS2\displaystyle=4e^{-2K_{+}\tilde{u}(u)}\big(1-f(r(u,\tilde{v}))\big)dud\tilde{v}+r^{2}(u,\tilde{v})\sigma_{S^{2}}
≕−ΩRNdS2​(u,v~)2​d​u​d​v~+r2​(u,v~)​σS2.\displaystyle\eqqcolon-\Omega^{2}_{\text{RNdS}}(u,\tilde{v})^{2}dud\tilde{v}+r^{2}(u,\tilde{v})\sigma_{S^{2}}.

Notice that 1−f⁡(r⁡(u,v~))1-f(r(u,\tilde{v})) is non-positive for r⁡(u,v~)∈[r−,r+]r(u,\tilde{v})\in[r_{-},r_{+}] (see [CGNS15a, section 3]), and that ℋRNdS+=\mathcal{H}_{\text{RNdS}}^{+}= {u~=−∞}={u=0}\{\tilde{u}=-\infty\}=\{u=0\}. We observe that:

v~+u~=r∗=12​K+​log⁡|r−r+|+O⁡(1),\tilde{v}+\tilde{u}=r^{*}=\frac{1}{2K_{+}}\log|r-r_{+}|+O(1),

for rr close to r+r_{+}. So, by decomposing 1−f1-f into the product of its roots, we have

1−f⁡(r)∼−e2​K+​(v~+u~), as ​r↗r+.1-f(r)\sim-e^{2K_{+}(\tilde{v}+\tilde{u})},\quad\text{ as }r\nearrow r_{+}.

Therefore:

ΩRNdS2∼e2​K+​v~, as ​r↗r+.\Omega^{2}_{\text{RNdS}}\sim e^{2K_{+}\tilde{v}},\quad\text{ as }r\nearrow r_{+}. (B.3)

We now compare this expression with (2.3). Assumption (A) in section 2.2, (2.19) and (5.4) give

Ω2​(0,v)=−4​ν​(0,v)∼e2​K+​v,∀v≥v0.\Omega^{2}(0,v)=-4\nu(0,v)\sim e^{2K_{+}v},\quad\forall\,v\geq v_{0}. (B.4)

This result holds for all initial data satisfying the assumptions of section 2.2 and also for Reissner-Nordström-de Sitter initial data5858 58 Namely the case in which ϖ0≡ϖ+\varpi_{0}\equiv\varpi_{+}, r⁡(0,v)≡r+r(0,v)\equiv r_{+}, Q0≡Q+Q_{0}\equiv Q_{+}, λ0≡0\lambda_{0}\equiv 0, κ0≡1\kappa_{0}\equiv 1 and Ω2​(0,v)=4​e2​K+​v\Omega^{2}(0,v)=4e^{2K_{+}v}. Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
